#3610. 5 Best New Movies And Shows To Stream This Weekend On Netflix, Apple TV, Hulu, And More (Nov. 6-8)

It's the first full weekend of November, the weather is finally turning truly chilly, and Halloweekend is in the rear-view mirror. Whether you went all-out on your costume last weekend or you elected to slap a nametag with a different moniker on your shirt and call it a day (which is my preferred way to celebrate Halloween if asked to do so), this weekend is perfect for staying in and curling up with a fresh series or movie. So, what's new on the big streamers?

Between Apple, Peacock, Hulu, and Netflix, there's a decent spate of new releases heading to streaming this weekend (and some of them even dropped earlier in the week). Whether you want to watch a gripping spy drama, a truly ridiculous legal drama, a breezy sports comedy, a crime thriller tinged with romance, or a quick-paced series featuring one of the best and weirdest pairings in TV history, I've got you covered.

Director Adam Carter Rehmeier, known for indie films like "Snack Shack" and "Dinner in America," teamed up with modern scream queen Samara Weaving and horror staple Kyle Gallner for this year's "Carolina Caroline" — which just hit Netflix, marking its first home on a major streaming service. Weaving, who also led "Ready or Not 2: Here I Come" and "Over Your Dead Body" recently (and who's joining the Marvel Cinematic Universe to play Emma Frost), stars as Caroline Daniels, a gas station attendant who falls in love with Gallner's con artist Oliver Anderson. As the two make their way to South Carolina from rural Texas, they end up committing robbery after robbery, leaving destruction in their wake.

Weaving's Caroline and Gallner's Oliver make for a great modern Bonnie and Clyde, and "Carolina Caroline" is a gripping, entertaining, and extraordinarily fun film that also features Jon Gries ("Napoleon Dynamite," "The White Lotus") and Kyra Sedgwick in supporting roles. If you want a crime drama packed with plenty of romance, "Carolina Caroline" on Netflix is your best bet.

Congratulations to all bad TV enjoyers: One of the worst shows ever made is back for Season 2! Ryan Murphy's gleefully ludicrous legal drama "All's Fair," which undoubtedly gives real lawyers raging headaches if they dare to tune in, stars Kim Kardashian as high-powered lawyer Allura Grant, who works alongside Liberty Ronson (Naomi Watts), Emerald J. Greene-Ball (Niecy Nash-Betts), Dina Standish (Glenn Close), and Milan (Teyana Taylor) at a firm that handles divorces. Sarah Paulson, a regular Murphy collaborator, livens up proceedings as rival lawyer Carrington "Carr" Lane, who is unbelievably twisted and extremely fun, and Nash-Betts, Watts, and Close are all game to ham it up.

I don't think I'm blowing anyone's mind when I say Kim Kardashian is a generationally dreadful actor who should not even appear in commercials, let alone a scripted drama that could be dishy and fun if she wasn't swanning around with absolutely zero expression in every single scene. Still, if you dig wildly bad TV and just want to switch your brain off, check out "All's Fair." Besides, if nothing else, it has given us an incredible episode of its fellow Hulu series "The Kardashians" where Close, out of character, gets very drunk off martinis at Kris Jenner's house.

I love "30 Rock," I have immense respect for weird little guy and short king Daniel Radcliffe, and I've been riding for Bobby Moynihan since the first time I saw him perform as Drunk Uncle on "Saturday Night Live." Essentially, "The Fall and Rise of Reggie Dinkins" — which stars Tracy Morgan, was created by Robert Carlock and Sam Means, is executive produced by Tina Fey, and stars Morgan and Radcliffe as the unlikeliest and best duo in recent TV memory — was made for me in a lab. My enduring affection for this show aside, I think it's sure to delight pretty much anybody, and when Season 1 premiered in January, it immediately became one of the best shows of 2026.

The premise? Morgan plays Reggie Dinkins, a disgraced NFL star who was banned from the New York Jets and all other professional teams in the league after being caught betting on his games. (Hilariously, he only bet on his own performance to inspire himself to play better.) Thus, Reggie tries to regain his tattered reputation alongside his best friend and former teammate Rusty (Moynihan), his ex-wife and manager Monica (Erika Alexander), his young but extremely compatible fiancée Brina (Precious Joy), his son Carmelo (Jalyn Hall), and Radcliffe's Oscar-winning documentarian Arthur Tobin. With Arthur living in his palatial suburban New York mansion to make a documentary that will hopefully relaunch Reggie's career and get him into the NFL Hall of Fame, Reggie does his best to refurbish his image, and the results are extremely funny. "Reggie Dinkins" Season 2 dropped on NBC and Peacock on November 2, and if you're returning to this near-perfect series, welcome back. If you're new, go laugh your way through Season 1, then join us.

If you enjoyed Keira Knightley and Ben Whishaw's delightful spy drama "Black Doves" when it dropped back on Netflix in 2024, you'll be pleased to hear the series — created by Joe Barton — released its second season on the streamer on November 5. Across six episodes, we pick up where the show left off with Helen Dawson (Knightley), a secret Black Doves operative who sells secrets to the highest bidder and also happens to be married to a Conservative MP for a major UK constituency and Secretary of State for Defense, Wallace Webb (Andrew Buchan). In the beginning of Season 1, Helen is shocked and saddened to learn that her lover, Jason Davies (Andre Koji), has died under suspicious circumstances ... and her secret identity may now be at risk.

Throughout that first season, Helen teams up with her old friend and hired assassin Sam Young (Whishaw), who's sent by the Doves to help protect her. In Season 2, after a shocking cliffhanger ending, we follow Helen and Sam as he desperately tries to keep her safe, even as she's targeted by nefarious forces throughout England. Knightley and Whishaw are fantastic together, and if you sort of forgot "Black Doves" was a thing since Season 1 premiered 2 years ago, I'm happy to tell you that it's back and still an extremely fun and enthralling watch.

Apple TV has some of the best comedy series on television hiding on its service (which seems to get overlooked in favor of ones like Netflix, Hulu, and Prime Video), and if you're a fan of "Ted Lasso" but haven't watched "Stick," you're really missing out. Owen Wilson leads this sports comedy created by Jason Keller and stars as Pryce Cahill, a former golf pro nicknamed "The Stick" who's stuck selling clubs and coaching at a country club after years of a career decline. At work one day, Pryce meets a gifted young golfer, Santi Wheeler (Peter Dager), who quit golfing after some personal issues got in the way of his game. Determined to make Santi the next golf star, Pryce ends up roping him into a cross-country tour to show off his talents alongside Santi's mother Elena (Mariana Treviño), Pryce's former caddy Mitts (Marc Maron), and a onetime bartender and current caddy Zero Duffy (Lili Kay), all of whom pile into an RV to make the trip.

"Stick" Season 2 adds great actors like Timothy Olyphant (as Pryce's former golf rival Clark Ross) as regulars and guest stars like recent Emmy winner Rhea Seehorn as Pryce's former coach, with Billy Zane also joining Season 2 in an as-yet-unknown capacity. The first two episodes of the sophomore season dropped on November 4, so catch up before it continues its run.

#3609. I Know Wildwood Isn't Doing Well At The Box Office, But I'm Just Happy It Exists In A World Of AI

Let me start off by saying that I LOVE Fathom Entertainment. In fact, I probably attend at least three Fathom Events a year. That said, when I saw that Laika's new movie, Wildwood, was being distributed by Fathom, my first thought was, Uh oh.

This is not a dig at Fathom. It's just that when I think of them, I picture watching Jaws on the big screen, or stuff from the Metropolitan Opera. So, I thought Laika must have had a difficult time finding a distributor with Wildwood. Well, it turns out that Laika chose Fathom specifically so that they wouldn't have to follow the regular Hollywood model.

Which is so Laika, i.e., badass. While Hollywood is veering deeper into AI territory, Laika bucks the trend, sticking to painstaking stop-motion animation. So, even if Wildwood isn’t a massive hit, here's why I'm just happy that it even exists.

When it comes to animation, there are three companies that I put above the rest. First is Studio Ghibli (obviously). Second is Pixar (another obvious choice), and third, well…my third choice might not be so obvious. I think it's because this particular company hasn't experienced the same seismic success as the other two, and that company is, of course, Laika.

While their catalogue might be paltry in comparison to the other two, I think all 5 of Laika's films prior to Wildwood are excellent. In fact, I remember when I first saw Coraline - which is still the company's most profitable movie - in theaters. My wife is a big fan of the book, and when the movie ended, she actually said it was one of the few instances where the movie was better than the book. She attributed this to the stop-motion animation, which she said added an extra layer of creepiness with how inherently jerky the movements are.

I agree. In fact, all of Laika's movies feel enhanced by the stop-motion animation. The Boxtrolls in particular feels like it couldn’t come from any other company. So, whenever a Laika movie comes out, there’s a good chance that I’m going to love it.

Book-to-screen adaptations can be conventional, or they can be something completely different. Take the Harry Potter movies, for instance. Yes, there were details left out of the films, but otherwise, they were pretty much by-the-book (pun not intended) adaptations. Same goes for The Hunger Games movies. If you read the novels, then you got pretty much the same thing with the films.

Wildwood, however, is an unconventional book with an unconventional adaptation. Written by The Decemberists frontman, Colin Meloy, and illustrated by his wife, Carson Ellis, Wildwood is a story where Portland, Oregon is just as important a backdrop as the magical fantasy world that’s presented in the story. The catalyst for the adventure is a child abduction by crows, and it’s a winding tale that gets more intriguing the deeper it goes.

Sure, a movie adaptation COULD have just had traditional animation, or could have even been live-action, but there’s just something special with this particularly unique story - which can be quite scary - being told in Laika’s trademark style. It works.

Lastly, even if Wildwood doesn’t do massive numbers at the box office, can’t we all just be happy that it’s not just some AI slop?

Wildwood is the studio’s longest movie at 132 minutes, as well as the longest stop-motion movie ever made. It also took SIXTEEN FREAKING YEARS TO MAKE! Now THAT’S dedication! The fact that Wildwood even exists seems to be a modern-day miracle, as studios have been gravitating towards more and more AI in their films. I applaud Travis Knight and the whole Laika crew for dedicating their lives to being true to their art form.

So, kudos to Laika and their new movie, Wildwood. Thank you for keeping true art (minus AI) alive.

Rich is a Jersey boy, through and through. He graduated from Rutgers University (Go, R.U.!), and thinks the Garden State is the best state in the country. That said, he’ll take Chicago Deep Dish pizza over a New York slice any day of the week. Don’t hate. When he’s not watching his two kids, he’s usually working on a novel, watching vintage movies, or reading some obscure book.

#3608. How the Newly Elected Congress Can Save the Smithsonian

This is the November 6, 2026 edition of True Colors, a look inside the global deals and colorful critiques that make the art world go round, with a weekly guide to the must-see openings, auctions, and fairs.

It’s True Colors. The Democrats have flipped the House and the Senate, which could usher in a new era of funding at the Smithsonian—or, at the very least, a vibe shift in DC. There are a ton of gallery shows opening around New York, and on the West Coast, LACMA Art+Film Gala goes down tomorrow night. We got the rare chance to sit down with one of the night’s honorees, Vija Celmins.

Mentioned in this issue: Donald Trump, Lonnie Bunch, Alma Allen, Tilman Fertitta, Yoshitomo Nara, Loïc Gouzer, Vija Celmins, Matthew Marks, Leonardo DiCaprio, Eva Chow, Denis Villeneuve, Gary Hume, Jacqueline Tran, Michael Govan, Katherine Ross, James Turrell, Riko Mizuno, Matthew Barney, Roni Horn, Meshell Ndegeocello, Steve McQueen, Matthieu Blazy, Rosemarie Trockel, Carrie Mae Weems, Marina Abramović, Wade Guyton, Christopher Wool, Rashid Johnson, Felix Rödder, Calvin Marcus, James Ensor.

Trump has spent the last two years attacking Washington’s cultural hub with executive orders and legally dubious firings issued via fiat. But the Smithsonian gets its funding through Congress—what if Congress actually acted on that authority?

Sure, Congress has more pressing issues to address once the deeply blue House and Senate get sworn in early next year. But here at True Colors I think it’s fair to ask the question: Will lawmakers wind back the years of impact the Trump administration has had on the Smithsonian Institution?

Although Congress has authority over the cultural behemoth, the White House has in just the last two years issued executive orders, been extremely hands-on in its public signage, and mounted pressure campaigns to fire directors and censor artworks. Congress could have stopped all of this, but didn't. Republicans naturally didn’t want to cross Trump and support the beleaguered arts mecca. But Democrats have every reason to—after the new Congress is sworn in they’ll have the power to appropriate massive amounts of funding to each Smithsonian museum—or even create new museums. Plus, that can impact how the whole institution is run on a day-to-day basis, as Congress has the power to shake up the Smithsonian’s board of regents. That governing body will choose the next Smithsonian secretary, after Lonnie Bunch resigned earlier this year.

I’m particularly interested in who takes over as the director of the Hirshhorn Museum and Sculpture Garden. Melissa Chiu, who held the position for 12 years, stepped down earlier this year to be the director of the Guggenheim Museum in New York, and rumors are swirling about who will succeed her in the post. The prospect of a culture-living Congress—and, who knows...a Democratic president come 2029?—could make the Smithsonian seem like a swell place to be long term.

Add in the prospect of a new crop of congressional staffers and the attendant cottage industries of consultants and lobbyists all flocking to Washington, and I could see the Hirshhorn getting caught up in the vibe shift, pronto. There’s expected to be a sea change of DC residents in town, and there’s every reason to believe they’ll make the (free! always free!) contemporary art museum a constant stop on the rotation. Plus, the long-gestating renovation of the Sculpture Garden literally just opened this past weekend. I don’t have any inside intel on who’s in the running for the job —but it’s looking like a pretty great gig these days.

Read True Colors: Inside the global deals and colorful critiques that make the art world go round, with a weekly guide to the must-see openings, auctions, and fairs.

Meanwhile, the artworks that filled the American Pavilion at the Venice Biennale, made by State Department–tapped artist Alma Allen, might be stuck in Italy for the foreseeable future. Funding has run out, and there’s nothing in the budget for moving the works. I wonder how that can be resolved. Seems like a job for an art-loving, restaurant-owning Italian ambassador, Tilman Fertitta!

The massive two-location Yoshitomo Nara show opened at David Zwirner last night, truly one of the great gallery moments here in New York this season. Don’t miss the pop-up one-painting exhibition of Nara’s In the Milky Lake / Thinking One, which will be sold by Loïc Gouzer’s one-lot auction business, Fair Warning. It’s on view at 534 W. 22nd Street. The lot opens for live bidding November 19 and is expected to sell for the eye-popping sum of $10 million to $15 million.

You can also see Nara’s work in Washington, DC, where the aforementioned Hirshhorn just opened a grand survey of the artist timed to the inauguration of its sculpture garden. And if you want to check out some of Nara’s artworks in a very unexpected place, head to the Avenue A dive bar Niagara, where Nara drunkenly created a masterwork on the walls late one night after an opening at Pace. The bar wisely conserved the artwork behind glass, and it remains there nearly two decades later.

It’s not usually worth reporting on the toasts given at gala dinners here in the prized real estate that is this newspaper’s Table Hopping section, but the Dia Fall Night had some good honorary toast content! On Monday, Matthew Barney proved himself to be a very deep Roni Horn fan with his toast. Then Meshell Ndegeocello went super outside the box, honoring Steve McQueen by stepping in front of the podium and leading a band around the gala. The whole evening was like that. Chanel wasn’t just a sponsor—the brand’s creative director Matthieu Blazy, a true contemporary art head, chaired the whole thing alongside artists Rosemarie Trockel and Carrie Mae Weems. Marina Abramović was at my table; she told me she reads Vanity Fair every time she’s on a plane and appreciates how thick the issues have been lately. Marina, it’s an honor. Thank you for reading.

Matthew Marks hosted a party on Wednesday night for Wade Guyton’s excellent new show at Bridges, the best restaurant on Chatham Square. Fun fact: Christopher Wool’s old studio was right next to the restaurant some decades back.

On Election Day, as the results started coming in, Rashid Johnson opened a show of new work at Hauser & Wirth’s Wooster Street gallery, which has recently become my favorite of the mega-gallery’s dozen or so global outposts. It’s a throwback of sorts, a small space in the neighborhood that was once the city’s gallery nexus, with an excellent track record of great shows. The dinner was at the gallery’s restaurant, Manuela, right around the corner on Prince Street. There was caviar, and while it was served to celebrate Johnson, it happened to come out right as the news networks indicated the Democrats were going to flip a Senate seat in South Carolina. Spirits were high.

If you’re making your way to The Met to see “Krasner and Pollock: Past Continuous,” do stop by Rodder, the gallery founded by Felix Rödder, to see one of the most inspired artist pairings in the city right now. Calvin Marcus, the fanatically talented and free-wheeling Los Angeles painter, has new and recent paintings, drawings, and ceramics installed alongside work by the great Belgian weirdo James Ensor. The chemistry between these two artists from different centuries and continents is uncanny. The dinner for the show was held somewhere unusual: House of the Redeemer, the Episcopalian Church in a former Italian Renaissance Revival townhouse once owned by a Vanderbilt heiress.

#3607. Your Discord Messages Will Soon Be Discoverable on Google Search, but You Can Opt Out

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

If you are a member of a large public Discord, your posts may soon be visible in Google Search—even to those without a Discord account. Starting in November, Discord's Discoverable Servers will have server web pages that show up in web search results, including summaries and messages from public channels. While messages won't be tied to your username or avatar, you may still want to opt out.

This change applies to Discoverable Servers on Discord, which are public spaces that have at least 1,000 members. There's no invite link, so anyone can find and join them as long as they have a Discord account. (Other servers on Discord are either invite-only Community Servers for larger groups or Friend Servers, which are small, private spaces.)

On Nov. 16, Discord is launching server web pages for Discoverable Servers, which will display discussion summaries from public channels as well as some individual messages. By mid-December, these pages may appear in search results. While these servers have always been fairly easy to access since they are public, this removes the requirement to sign up for Discord and join servers in order to view them.

In its announcement detailing the change, Discord notes that private servers and DMs will remain private. Plus, server admins can choose which channels are included in web search or opt them out entirely.

Messages you send before mid-December won't be included in search regardless of your setting preferences. However, if you leave this enabled and decide to turn it off later, anything you send between mid-December and disabling the setting will stay up unless you delete the message from Discord entirely.

#3606. The 8 Best Castlevania Games Of All Time, Ranked

Castlevania is one of the most beloved franchises in video game history, despite a period of 13 years when we didn’t see a new installment until the launch of Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse earlier this year.

Over the years, the games have provided a variety of experiences, mixed with rich lore built on the vampire myth. With so many games available to choose from, it can be difficult to know where to begin if you haven’t touched the series in a while. Accordingly, here is our ranked list of the 8 best Castlevania games. It should make an excellent starting point.

When Castlevania came to the Super Nintendo, it needed to impress players who were still deciding whether they wanted to spend money on a new generation of Nintendo hardware. Fortunately for everyone involved, the team at Konami was up to the task. Super Castlevania 4 features beautiful environments, as well as a hero who can now whip in eight directions, even while jumping. It’s also possible to grapple to distant points, or to wield the whip as a shield. Early use of Mode 7 rotation provided some visual showpieces to go along with parallax depth that brought static environments to life. The adventure starts outside the castle, allowing Simon to explore its harsh exterior before venturing inside for a final showdown with the lord of the manor. If you’re looking for a starting point, you could do much worse, and it’s conveniently available as part of the Castlevania Anniversary Collection on Switch, PlayStation 4, PC, and Xbox One.

The Super Nintendo wasn’t the only hardware to feature a high-quality Castlevania game during the 16-bit era. Castlevania: Bloodlines took a unique approach, introducing a hero who strikes with a spear. He can use it to access alternate routes that the other character (who fights with a more traditional whip) cannot. The pacing was fast and furious, in keeping with many Genesis games of that time. The setting was also more modern than the other classic titles, taking place during the first World War. Stages are inspired by locations around the globe, including a visit to the Leaning Tower of Pisa, among other attractions. Throw in some stunning visual tricks that made full use of the Genesis hardware, along with a beautiful score from composer Michiru Yamane (who would go on to compose for Symphony of the Night) and you have a truly special entry in the franchise.

Originally developed for the Sharp X68000 and released on that hardware as Akumajo Dracula, Castlevania Chronicles was one of the final Castlevania games built in the classical style. It actually is a remake of 1986’s first entry in the series. 1993’s version offered greatly improved visuals and sound, while providing generally fair but challenging gameplay that is some of the most difficult the series ever offered. Some new twists maintain the element of surprise, even as players retread familiar ground, but there’s no better way to experience the original adventure, as its developers intended. When I checked earlier this year, the digital version of the prettied up PlayStation port was still available to purchase through the PlayStation Store on a PlayStation 3 console, if you add the funds to your wallet on newer hardware. Or you can hunt down a physical copy of that port, which should play just fine on your PlayStation 3.

If more people had easily been able to play the game as its developers intended, Castlevania: Rondo of Blood might be remembered today as the premier Castlevania experience. Sadly, the game remained exclusive to the PC Engine CD hardware for a long time. It didn’t head to North America and Europe until it arrived on PSP as part of 2007’s Castlevania: The Dracula X Chronicles collection, and as a Virtual Console selection in 2010, almost a decade and a half after its initial release. The closest we got in the meantime was Dracula X on the Super Nintendo. That title was a mostly unsuccessful attempt to compress Rondo of Blood’s essence to fit on a cartridge — and to reach hardware that hadn’t bombed outside of Japan. The same plot and characters returned, as did many enemy sprites. Both games began in a town on fire. However, the branching stages were absent, replaced by abbreviated challenges that players found frustrating. Some characters from the original version weren’t even playable, and the sound quality suffered immensely. Rondo of Blood is an important game in Castlevania’s timeline, and concludes with the events that serve as a prologue to Symphony of the Night. If you haven’t yet done so, you should play through it soon.

Castlevania: Aria of Sorrow followed one year after Harmony of Dissonance, which in some respects was the more spectacular of the pair. But despite its inferior visuals, Aria of Sorrow offered the richer experience on a mechanical level. Players control Soma Cruz, who blacks out during the first solar eclipse of the century and awakens in Dracula’s castle. There, he finds he can absorb the essence of the monsters he vanquishes, a useful way to gain the strength he’ll need to reach Dracula’s throne room and rescue his classmate. The adventure is surprisingly complex, given the tiny hardware that houses it, and still a lot of fun to play. You can most easily experience it and other games of that era as part of Castlevania Advance Collection on Switch, PlayStation 4, PC, and Xbox One.

A weekly cheat sheet to what you’ll eventually love to play. No buying, no commitment — just saving for later.

The 8-bit era established Castlevania as a force to be reckoned with, ensuring it survived long enough to continue breaking new ground over the decades. But those early titles aren’t always a lot of fun to play today. The original game sometimes felt cheap and rather bland, even near release. Its sequel had an interesting plot and ambitious new mechanics, but it confounded many players with unclear, non-linear objectives. Then Castlevania 3: Dracula’s Curse came around and perfected the formula, providing multiple heroes with lore (which Netflix later explored with an animated series) and unique play styles, along with diverging paths through gorgeous stages that pushed the NES hardware harder than ever before. It’s the finest single example of what Castlevania could be during that era, and well worth revisiting today.

Check our full Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse review for all the details, but the short version is this: you need to play the game. It respects the series’ history while mapping out a potential future we hope the developers will one day realize with follow-up titles. The 2.5D visuals give each area a new sense of depth, while enabling the satisfying Metroidvania mechanics players have enjoyed since Symphony of the Night changed the franchise forever. Fluid movement during combat, a killer soundtrack to match the moonlit ambience of the visuals, and a brave new hero all add up to one of the very finest entries the series has ever seen.

Nearly 30 years after its release, there’s still no topping Castlevania: Symphony of the Night. It’s the game credited with taking Metroid’s design and fusing it with the gothic adventuring players associate with the Castlevania series. The sprawling castle was populated by nightmarish creatures, many of them familiar and many of them not. Stripped of his powerful weapons, Alucard explores the castle and seeks to put down his fearsome father once and for all. But as players learned, there’s much more to the adventure than the simple castle they glimpse beneath the moonlight. One of the happiest surprises in video games came when players looked at things through a new perspective, thanks to some holy spectacles. The shift in focus opened up an unfamiliar pathway, revealing that they weren’t even halfway done with their adventure. It was the game that kept on giving, and it still hasn’t stopped.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#3605. 5 Years Ago: Benedict Cumberbatch Starred In Netflix's Best Western Movie

Jane Campion's 2021 film "The Power of the Dog," released five years ago this month, was one of the best films of its year. It was widely praised by critics and by the Academy, despite earning a tiny handful of cash during its not-very-wide theatrical release. The film was nominated for an astonishing 12 Academy Awards, including Best Picture, making it the seventh Netflix film in four years to be nominated in the top category (other nominees included "Roma," "The Irishman," "Marriage Story," "Mank," "The Trial of the Chicago 7," and "Don't Look Up"). "The Power of the Dog" ultimately only won one Oscar, for Best Director.

The film takes place on a ranch in Montana in the mid-1920s, owned by brothers Phil and George Burbank (Benedict Cumberbatch and Jesse Plemons). Kirsten Dunst plays Rose, the proprietress of a local inn, who is raising her teenage son Peter (Kodi Smit-McPhee) by herself. Early in the film, Phil admires that Rose's dining tables are decorated with paper flowers, but becomes a little grossed out when he learns that Peter was the one who constructed them. This little observation kicks off the movie's powerful themes about traditional masculinity, gender dynamics, and the place of queerness on the open frontier.

These four characters get swirled together when George marries Rose and Phil's cruel nature reveals itself. While the young Peter leaves to go to medical school, Rose finds herself under pressure — more from Phil than from George — to be a "woman of the house." Phil insists, for instance, that Rose play the piano at a fancy dinner party, something she can't bear to do. By the time Peter comes home for a break, Rose has begun to hit the bottle.

We soon learn that both Phil and the young Peter are likely queer. Peter is more openly so, as he becomes fascinated by a secret stash of magazines full of hunky dudes. Phil, meanwhile, is very fond of a scarf that once belonged to the now-dead Bronco Henry, his former mentor ... and possibly more. Eventually, Phil begins to take Peter under his wing. Later in the film, Phil tacitly admits that Bronco Henry once saved his life during a blizzard by holding their nude bodies together. It's all but stated outright that Phil and Bronco Henry were lovers. This is the 1920s in rural Montana, however, so these men don't seem to have the freedom, nor even the vocabulary, to express their queerness.

At home, meanwhile, Rose's life is falling apart. She's drinking more and more, and her relationship with Phil is fraught. Although Phil eventually warms to Peter, he seems to place all his self-hate onto Rose, mocking her and making her life as miserable as possible. Phil is blaming Rose, it seems, for forcing him to reckon with his attraction to men. This leads to a late-film twist about rope-making and anthrax that leaves the film on a very dark note indeed.

"The Power of the Dog" is a marvelous tragedy of pain, self-denial, and gender roles. Rose cannot be the "sweet little wife," and Phil masks his need to be gentle and "soft" by affecting a "grizzled" exterior. Cumberbatch is fantastic in the role of Phil, capturing both his character's cruelty and his hidden gentleness. The film's title comes from Psalms, 22:20: "Deliver my soul from the sword, my precious life from the power of wild dogs."

Jane Campion's filmography is full of bangers, going back to her early films like "Sweetie" and "An Angel at My Table," through "The Piano" and "Portrait of a Lady," and up to "Bright Star" and "The Power of the Dog." This has been her most recent film to date.

Critics loved this movie, which earned a 94% approval rating on Rotten Tomatoes based on 363 reviews. /Film wrote that Cumberbatch delivered a career-best performance. Meanwhile, The New York Times' Manohla Dargis loved the sweep of the film as well as its treatment of the Phil character, a man who, she observed, had been "playing" a cowboy for decades of his life. About the film's visuals, Dargis wrote:

"A bold visual stylist, Campion introduces this world and its people with sweep and precision, with soaring eagle-eye aerial shots and her characteristic attention to voluptuary detail (and with New Zealand doubling for an unspoiled Montana). She fluently sets the western milieu, with its swirling dust and thundering cattle, and catches the boisterous camaraderie of the ranch hands, the playfulness of their jostling with its easy, unselfconscious physicality and intimacy."

/Film's Joshua Meyer wrote a full explanation of the ending of "The Power of the Dog," realizing that it's a tale of emotional terrorism and that it may be freeing to wriggle out from under the masculine lifestyle Phil was trying to perpetuate. "The Power of the Dog" was based on the novel by Thomas Savage, and Campion, who also wrote the adaptation, changed the ending (we think for the better). In Campion's version, the themes are incredibly clear, very moving, and pointedly righteous.

#3604. If You Loved 'East of Eden,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

One of the best things about truly great stories is how they can be endlessly adapted and reinterpreted. John Steinbeck published “East of Eden” in 1952, and each time it’s adapted to a screen, it looks a little different. Netflix’s try at this huge, complex story offers up some searing performances, especially from Florence Pugh as the notorious Cathy Ames. Ames is one of the best characters ever crafted in American literature, but her sociopathic nature has sometimes made her into a simple villain—but the series, and Pugh's performances, adds depth to the charcter. If the limited series has you wanting more complex female characters from classic novels, your next move is obvious: Vanity Fair, starring Reese Witherspoon as Becky Sharp.

First published in the mid-19th century, “Vanity Fair” by William Makepeace Thackeray is an enduring classic of American literature, satirizing the artificial manners and pretensions of Victorian society. At the center of the story is Becky Sharp, whose moral ambiguity and self-serving actions were surprising and unexpected at the time—and have made her a kind of antihero in the modern age. Sharp is a complicated character who, like Cathy Ames, can easily be flattened into a villain, a social climber who uses people.

The 2004 adaptation leans into the more modern take on Sharp’s character, giving her more justification for her actions and humanizing her more than the novel. Sharp is orphaned at a young age, but is almost feral in her determination to secure a position in society—which, at the time, meant securing an advantageous marriage. The story doesn’t have the same sweep as East of Eden, chronicling a relatively short period of time—but that period is the Napoleonic Wars, so there’s a lot going on. This gives the film a similarly epic feel even as it focuses on Sharp’s constant scheming and endless flirtations with people who she thinks can help her out.

In many ways, Sharp is simply playing by the rules imposed on her by men, and if that was scandalous in 1848, it’s almost heroic by today’s standards, and Reese Witherspoon imbues her Sharp with a bit of grace to reflect that. But she’s still someone who does what she must to survive and thrive, and that prickly edge will appeal to fans of Pugh in East of Eden. Rent Vanity Fair on Prime Video.

Need more historical epics with fascinating, complex characters? Luckily, the movies tend to specialize in that—here are a few more movies that fans of East of Eden will love.

If you thought the best thing about East of Eden was Florence Pugh, you’re going to love Lady Macbeth. Pugh plays Katherine, a young woman pushed into an arranged marriage with wealthy landowner Alexander Lester (Paul Hilton) in England in 1865. The marriage is solely intended to produce an heir, and Katherine is initially imprisoned in the house. When Alexander and his father leave Katherine alone for some time, she walks the estate and begins a brazen affair with a worker, setting off a chain of violent events that gets bleaker with each scene. Pugh’s portrayal of another dark, determined woman is mesmerizing. Stream Lady Macbeth on Kanopy or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

If you want more sprawling family drama in a historical setting, look no further than Legends of the Fall. Set in the early 20th century, it follows Colonel William Ludlow (Anthony Hopkins) and his sons Tristan (Brad Pitt), Alfred (Aidan Quinn), and Samuel (Henry Thomas) as they navigate life choices and deal with the emotional wounds they inflict on each other. From World War I to Prohibition, the Ludlows fall in love (sometimes with each other’s wives), suffer crushing loss, and remain connected to their ranch and the natural beauty of Montana through it all. Anchored by a star turn by Brad Pitt, this movie will scratch the itch left behind by East of Eden. Rent Legends of the Fall on Prime Video.

If you want to see a different take on the novel, check out the 1955 adaptation directed by Elia Kazan (grandfather of Zoe Kazan, who co-wrote and directed the 2026 series). Starring James Dean (who would die a few months after its release), it’s an old-school Hollywood epic that only covers the final third of the book. That makes it a very different narrative experience from the series, which has more room to explore the novel’s complexities—but the film looks amazing, Dean’s performance is terrific, and Kazan directs the heck out of it. Rent East of Eden on Prime Video.

Another choice for epic family drama, Giant was James Dean’s last film, and offers family drama in heaps. Like East of Eden, it follows a family over the course of decades as patriarch Jordan “Bick” Benedict, Jr. (Rock Hudson) tries to maintain his family’s ranching legacy in the face of changing times and a flood of oil money, while his former ranch hand Jett Rink (Dean) pines for Bick’s wife, Leslie (Elizabeth Taylor), and strikes it rich with oil. As money’s corrosive effect takes its toll on Jett, the Benedict family grows and changes, with plenty of drama to spare along the way. Rent Giant on Prime Video.

If East of Eden makes you curious about other adaptations of Steinbeck’s work, your next stop should be John Ford’s 1940 version of The Grapes of Wrath. Set during the Great Depression, it follows Tom Joad (Henry Fonda) after his release from prison for manslaughter. He finds his family has been forced off their land, and joins them in a desperate migration to California in hopes of finding work and security. Along the way, Joad kills again and undergoes what can only be described as radicalization, dedicating his life to organizing labor and fighting back against the predations of capitalist society. It’s a remarkable film pulsing with emotional heft and deep family drama, and if its story and setting are very different from East of Eden, the impact will be similar. Stream The Grapes of Wrath on Hoopla, or rent it on Prime Video.

#3603. 23 Years Later, Buddy The Elf's Best Line Is Still The Greatest Christmas Quote Ever

When "Elf" came out in 2003, it established itself as an immediate Christmas classic, and on the movie's 23rd anniversary, we want to celebrate a simple, effective line from this Will Ferrell comedy which is not only fun for the whole family, but which has stood the test of time.

Before we get to the line in question, though, let's go over the basics where "Elf" is concerned. Directed by Jon Favreau (the Marvel and Star Wars one, not the political guy) and written by David Berenbaum, who wrote the movie after an earlier project called "Christmas in New Jersey" failed to take flight, "Elf" stars Ferrell as Buddy the titular elf, a human who's raised at the North Pole by his adoptive elf dad, Papa Elf (Bob Newhart, who also narrates the film). When Buddy sets out to find his birth father on the magical, mystical island of Manhattan, he meets Walter Hobbs (James Caan), a cynical and uptight publisher of children's books who isn't super interested in dealing with any large adult son, let alone one dressed like a Christmas elf who pours sugar on his spaghetti. Thankfully, Walter's wife and son, Emily and Michael (Mary Steenburgen and Daniel Tay), love Buddy, so he's accepted into the Hobbs household and ends up saving Christmas.

There are a lot of great "Elf" quotes — and we'll feature a bunch of them shortly — but the one I really want to center is one that expresses Buddy's worldview perfectly. So what is it?

While talking to his coworker and eventual girlfriend Jovie (Zooey Deschanel), Buddy, trying to get her to sing in public, tells her, "The best way to spread Christmas cheer is singing loud for all to hear." Not only is this just a nice, neat little rhyme, it's also the entire essence of the movie.

Sure, Buddy can be annoying, loud, and weird; a grown man in an elf costume is a concept that's great on screen and would be objectively terrifying in real life. (It adds to the cinematic hilarity and imagined real-life horror that Will Ferrell is well over six feet tall.) Still, Buddy's big heart and intense joy ends up making everyone believe in the magic of the holiday season — even Walter, who eventually accepts Buddy as his son and decides that he wants to spend more time with Emily and Michael in the process.

"Elf" is truly a movie about allowing yourself to indulge in joy and cheer, and this Buddy quote is basically the film's thesis. That's not the only quotable line from "Elf," though; there are so many others.

#3602. 12 Episodes Of The BBC's Murder Mystery Series Deliver The Cleverest Whodunnits On TV

Dipping your toe into British murder-mystery TV can be intimidating, but fortunately, one of the genre's most recent additions is also one of the best. There really are British murder mystery shows for everyone, ranging from the gritty and dark like Broadchurch to cozy comfort watches like Midsommar Murders. However, at 26 seasons and 144 episodes in, Midsomer Murders is, suffice it to say, a bit of a time commitment.

Fortunately, for those looking for a weekend binge on the cozier side, there's the BBC's Ludwig. Premiering in 2024, Ludwig centers on John "Ludwig" Taylor (David Mitchell), a reclusive and introverted puzzlemaker whose detective chief inspector twin brother, James (also Mitchell), goes missing. James' wife and John's childhood friend, Lucy (Anna Maxwell Martin), is desperate for his help in finding her husband, so John assumes James' identity to investigate. As he does, John becomes increasingly embroiled in real police work, as his puzzle skills translate perfectly to solving murder cases.

Ludwig was such a smash hit for the BBC that it was renewed for season 3 before its second season even premiered in August 2026. (A Christmas special is also coming later this year.) Not only does the fish-out-of-water comedy surrounding John's situation make Ludwig stand out, but the series' whodunnit mysteries are some of the cleverest that TV has ever seen.

Detective interrogation and forensic evidence are a dime a dozen in whodunnit TV shows. That's not a knock on them. Tropes are tropes for a reason — they're entertaining — and there are also myriad series offering fresh takes on the familiar. However, Ludwig's whodunnits are wholly unique, and one of the best parts of the series.

John is a socially awkward man with no scientific background — he's not going to be grilling suspects or gathering DNA evidence. Instead, he solves murder cases by treating them as puzzles, from logic grids to reverse chess, and that's infinitely more fun and clever to watch. It also invites viewers to play along and solve the case, unlike traditional police procedurals in which the killer can be guessed by following familiar story beats — or if they happen to be a famous guest star.

Ludwig season 2 is as comforting, fun, and watchable as ever. David Mitchell and Anna Maxwell Martin's amateur sleuths are an absolute delight.

Ludwig's killer reveal scenes are also as hilarious as they are brilliant. John detests most social interactions, so having to deliver a murder verdict to a room full of suspects and colleagues is torture for him, even though he has the killer dead to rights. It's a humorous inversion of a murder mystery climax that still satisfies diehard fans of these cozy stories.

While Ludwig's whip-smart writers could probably come up with enough puzzle-centric mysteries to fill a dozen seasons, James's disappearance is the show's main storyline, and it can only go on for so long. If Ludwig keeps dragging it out, it risks losing credibility and slackening the narrative tension; if it's not solved at some point, audiences will grow frustrated and stop caring. However, once the James mystery is over, so is the show, whether it ends on a happy note or a tragic one.

As tempting as it is to wish for Ludwig to become the next Midsomer Murders and run for dozens of seasons, that's just not the way it's designed. That's not a bad thing, and it doesn't make one series better or worse than the other. John "Ludwig" Taylor is a man who marches to the beat of his own drum and does things his way, and viewers love him for it — even if that means his show ends sooner rather than later.

#3601. 10 Fun and Quirky iPhone Duo Apps Worth Checking Out

The launch of the iPhone Duo marks the first time that Apple has fundamentally changed the form factor of the iPhone. This is an exciting development because, among other reasons, it allows app developers to get even more creative. If you have an iPhone Duo, plan to get one, or if you're just interested in creative app interfaces, then you should take a look at these apps.

With Tiny Computers ($4), when you use the Duo half-open, it turns the bottom display into a keyboard, and the screen goes up top. The app features computers inspired by Commodore 64, Windows 95, iMac G3, Macintosh, IBM PC, Amiga 500, ThinkPad, iBook G3, Powerbook G4, and Windows XP. The attention to detail is great, but early App Store reviews mention that the app can be buggy.

I miss the tactile nature of playing music on my cassette player at home, and my old Sony Walkman clone. Deck-Man ($5) is an app that brings the Walkman's interface, complete with all the clicks and clacks, to your iPhone Duo. Each time you play an album, Deck-Man lets you "insert" the cassette in the player before it starts playing. The app links to your Apple Music account and it also supports playing local music files.

Foldissimo (free, $10 to unlock all songs) simulates the sound of airflow in an accordion as you fold and unfold your iPhone Duo. It has some songs pre-loaded, and you can pay $10 to unlock all songs. Foldissimo also supports a few other instruments (accordion organ, panpipes, and theremin), but you'll need to pay an additional $10 to unlock those.

With Flipcorder ($5), while the viewfinder and the retro interface are visible to you when you have the Duo in tablet mode, your subjects can also see the frame via the outer display. When you fold the Duo, the app saves the clip, and allows you to record up to 30 minutes of video per day, each of which is saved in a virtual "tape."

Orisuji ($5) is a puzzle game where you solve mazes by folding your iPhone Duo. It has 69 levels, and you'll be solving most of these by folding or unfolding the device to shift the position of the maze to make your characters move, unlock doors, or to find keys to get past locked doors.

Toastie ($3) is a game where you, well, make sandwiches: It has 10 recipes for you to master, with a time limit of 15 seconds per step as your in-game customers wait for you to serve them. You fold the phone to "cook" the sandwich; leave it folded for too long and you'll end up with burnt toast.

Marbles Unhinged (Free, $3/each to unlock all levels in a world) is a puzzle game where you guide a marble towards the exit in each level. When you fold your iPhone, it turns the top half of the level into a ramp, and alters the speed of the marble. You can keep the phone at different angles to change the nature of the stage, which will lead you to the solution.

ChompDuo (Free, $1 to unlock all monsters) uses the Duo's folding mechanics to make monsters "chomp" down, and you'll feel each bite via haptic vibrations. When you close the Duo, the monster's eyes stare at you from the outer display. It's a silly app that you or your kids could enjoy playing around with.

Unfold Your City (Free, $5 to unlock all cities) simulates pop-up books to guide you through the highlights of different cities. It reminds me of Robert Sabuda's beautiful pop-up books, especially when you use the app on iPhone Duo. It slowly pops up the artwork for each city as you unfold the device, and displays the cover when you close the "book."

In the Pokémon anime, the Pokédex is an encyclopedia that catalogs information about your friendly neighborhood pocket monsters. Dex Fold (Free, $3 to unlock optional features) simulates the device from the anime, which means that you can only use the app when you unfold the iPhone Duo.

#3600. 38 Years Later, Calvin and Hobbes' Lost Character Remains Bill Watterson's Biggest Failure

The Lyman of Calvin and Hobbes, if you will

The author Lois McMaster Bujold has said that “the writer should always reserve the right to come up with a better idea.” That's a useful guideline for any reader to keep in mind. As any long-form story evolves, it usually picks up a few dead plot branches or abandoned characters, because the author can exercise their option to drop what they're doing for any (or no) reason. Sometimes it's not a continuity error; it's a deliberate change in direction.

Sometimes that decision is due to unexpected popularity, like how Opus and Bill the Cat quickly stole the spotlight in Bloom County. At other times, it might be due to shifting creative teams, real life concerns (i.e. Stephen King's near-death experience in 1999 became a major plot element of the last two books of his Dark Tower series), or that the author simply pivoted away from a plan that wasn't going to work out.

Bill Watterson's Calvin and Hobbes has surprisingly few of those abandoned plot threads. It starts in close to the same place as it ends, as a joke-a-day strip with occasional deviations into high weirdness, art criticism, and accessible philosophy. There's a little more focus on Calvin's parents in the first couple of years of C&H and the art's a little looser, but the comic stays close to its original vision through its 10-year run.

The only real exception is in a two-week arc from 1988, where Calvin's uncle Max comes to visit his household. On a blind read through the comic, it's nothing that unusual, but the behind-the-scenes story of Uncle Max is a little more interesting.

The "Uncle Max" arc ran from Jan. 11 to 22 in 1988, taking up the weekday strip for just under two weeks. The comics are collected in Calvin and Hobbes' third print collection, Yukon Ho!

Uncle Max's visit takes Calvin by surprise, as Max hasn't been around since Calvin was a baby, so Calvin doesn't remember him at all. While Calvin is initially suspicious of this new adult presence in his house, he eventually warms up to Max, if only because Max is the only other person in the strip who's willing to at least pretend he's scared of Hobbes.

Watterson doesn't give Max much in the way of a backstory. He's drawn like Calvin's dad with no glasses and a mustache. He also vaguely seems like he spent some time on the wrong side of the law. (When Calvin asks why Max hasn’t been around, Calvin’s dad says that the idea Max was in jail for a while “isn’t a bad guess.”) We don't learn what Max does for a living, why he's in town, or where he lives. Instead, he's simply there to bounce off of Calvin and his parents for a couple of weeks, and then he leaves. Max never appears again.

Watterson didn't publicly comment on Uncle Max until The Calvin and Hobbes Tenth Anniversary Book in 1995, which reprinted a selection of C&H strips alongside Watterson's essays and commentary. Since Watterson has been notoriously quiet since C&H ended in 1998, the Anniversary Book is still one of the only sources of behind-the-scenes information on C&H. If you're a fan of the comic, it's worth picking up a copy of the Anniversary Book, which is still in print via original publisher Andrews & McMeel.

According to Watterson in the Anniversary Book, his original plan for Uncle Max was to use him to expand the strip's scope. Max was going to appear again, and he'd potentially offer new stories where Calvin's family would go to visit him.

As Max's introductory arc continued, however, Watterson realized it wasn't going to work. For one thing, Calvin's parents' deliberate lack of names made it difficult to write dialogue between them and Max. More to the point, Max didn't offer as many options for new stories as Watterson had hoped he would. As a result, Watterson simply never used Uncle Max again, writing, "Max is gone."

That relegates Uncle Max to the realm of comic strip trivia, alongside other short-lived supporting characters like Lyman, Frieda, Hodge-Podge, or roughly three-quarters of the cast of Doonesbury. He was simply an idea that didn't work. Sometimes, that's just how things shake out in comics.

#3598. Five Hacks Every Suunto Race 3S User Should Know

Suunto's new Race 3S is a lightweight, premium racing watch—but at a retail price of $599, it's a steep climb from the Race S, which is regularly on sale for $299. Still, there are certainly some major upgrades: The battery holds 46% more than the Race S's, and it's good for up to 38 hours of dual-band GPS; storage is double the Race S's, at 64GB. And as always, with the SuuntoPlus store, you can download apps and integrations so your watch can do more than just the default features. After all, the best way to justify the price is to really make use of everything the watch can do. Here are five ways to get more out of your Suunto Race 3S.

(Suunto Race 3S users should also check out these Suunto Run hacks).

There are several ways you can explore new hikes, straight from your watch or app, and all from the comfort of your home. First up, make sure you download offline maps at home. The Race 3S offers free worldwide offline maps with contour lines and place names, and you pay no subscription. Download your regions over wifi before you leave, so you aren't relying on a phone signal at the trailhead. The 64GB of storage leaves room for several regions, so grab the places you actually run, plus anywhere you're traveling. Menu paths can shift with firmware updates, so check the Suunto app if the layout has changed.

From there, build a library of points of interest. A POI is any spot worth returning to, such as a trailhead, water source, campsite, or viewpoint—and with Suunto specifically, you get a broad definition of “POI,” including spots for hunting, fishing, foraging, or wildlife watching. There are built-in POI types for noting where a deer seemed to have rubbed its antlers, where you've seen marine mammals, or where you've spotted mushrooms. And with the Race 3S, you can store up to 250 of them on the watch.

You can create them on the map in the Suunto app without even being there in person, or when you do stumble upon one, you can save your current location from the watch mid-run. You just have to plug in the POI as a Navigation Target under the options for your trail run or other activity. There's also a navigation app, accessible from the bottom of the widget list (select All Apps), and you can navigate without having an activity running. Organize them by area before a hiking trip, and you can navigate to a trailhead or a spring with a few taps, with the map showing the terrain around you.

For all the hikers out there, you can use Climb Guidance to preview the climbs. When you load a route, Climb Guidance splits it into flat, uphill, downhill, climb and descent sections, and shows remaining ascent. Use it to decide where to push and where to hold back. It doesn't set your pace for you, but it lets you pace by terrain.

Suunto’s Race line includes a storm alarm that watches for rapid pressure drops, a warning sign that weather is turning. It only helps if the barometer reading is trustworthy, so set your altitude to a known reference (a trailhead sign or a verified elevation) before you head up. To turn on storm alerts, go into Settings > System notifications > Alerts > Storm. (This is also where you can set up sunrise and sunset notifications.)

Just remember to recalibrate your barometer every time you start from a new elevation. Also under the Settings menu, you can select Alti & Baro, and then you have the option to either Set altitude or Auto adjust altitude. The auto-adjustment uses a GPS reading to make sure the altimeter is calibrated. But if you know your current altitude from a map, you can set it manually.

Training by heart rate is a great idea, but the default zones on your watch are based on broad formulas and guesses. With the SuuntoPlus app store, you can select Anaerobic Threshold and follow the instructions to find the heart rate where effort turns hard, so your zones reflect your body.

Be prepared: A threshold test is a tough workout. After a warm-up, you’ll be asked to run as fast as you can for 30 minutes. At the end, the app will tell you the heart rate that seems to correspond with your lactate threshold.

Now here’s the cool part: On your watch, go into Settings, then Training, then Intensity zones. Choose either the Default HR zones for all sports (what I’d recommend if you aren’t sure) or choose a sport under the advanced setting. Here, you can set the boundaries between your zones. The boundary at the bottom of zone 5 (and thus the top of zone 4) should be set to the number you got from the threshold test. If you’d like to tweak the other zones, Suunto has more information on how to calculate numbers for the other zone boundaries.

And for any threshold test, where precision matters most, I recommend pairing with a chest strap.

SuuntoPlus apps run on the watch and show extra data during activities, and these two are worth setting up during your training:

Cadence Coach shows live cadence and stride length so you can work on running form and, in Suunto's words, avoid injuries. Run a few easy sessions with it, find the cadence that feels smooth, and use it as a target.

Sprint automatically records your strides and sprints, using wrist acceleration. Instead of tapping laps during strides or hill sprints, just run, and review the efforts afterward.

Activate both in the Suunto app's SuuntoPlus store before starting an exercise, and watch your running economy start to improve.

My favorite time-saving shortcut is to pin the timer widget. Widgets are reachable from the watch face by swiping up or turning the crown, and you can choose which ones to show and in what order in the Suunto app. Move the timer to the top, and pin it so a crown press opens it. Then the upper button starts and stops the stopwatch, and the lower button resets it. It's ideal for intervals, cooking, and race-day warm-ups, and you never have to start a full workout for a quick timing job. The timer remembers whether you last used the stopwatch or the countdown.

Finally, I’m keeping my eye on the launch of the Race Planner feature. It's meant to build a pacing plan from your route, weather, and goal time, and then guide your pace on race day. Suunto hasn't announced a date yet, so I wouldn’t exactly buy the watch for it.

#3597. James Gray on His ‘Only Real Beef with Streaming’ and the ‘Recurring Nightmare’ That Started at Cannes in 2009

James Gray time-travels back to his Queens roots once again for his latest film, “Paper Tiger.” It’s a location, an atmosphere, a state of mind he’s explored across decades and genres, dating back to his 1994 debut feature, “Little Odessa.” Like “Paper Tiger,” “Little Odessa” also featured the shadows of the Russian mafia looming over a family unit — to devastating ends. But even 30-plus years later, with his new movie — starring Miles Teller, Adam Driver, and Scarlett Johansson — Gray wanted to go just as dangerous.

Adam Driver, for one, has danger in him, according to Gray, who cast the Oscar nominee as a former police officer who links up with the red mafia in the 1980s. Gray recently joined IndieWire’s “Screen Talk” podcast hosts Anne Thompson and Ryan Lattanzio for a wide-ranging, amusingly discursive live conversation at the Virginia Film Festival. One that showcased his knack for impressions — from Luca Guadagnino beckoning Gray out of this year’s Cannes to sit down for the Italian filmmaker’s Bernardo Bertolucci documentary, to the waves of disappointment cresting through Maximilian Schell during an early Venice screening of “Little Odessa.” Related Stories How ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Used Real-World Sound to Make Its Monsters More Terrifying ‘Zi’ Review: Kogonada Rediscovers His Voice with a Microbudget Hong Kong Experiment Starring Michelle Mao and Haley Lu Richardson

“Almost all great performances have to have some measure of danger in them,” Gray said. “I can actually only think of one that doesn’t have any, which would probably be Jeff Bridges as The Dude in ‘The Big Lebowski,’ which has no danger at all.” (Though John Goodman’s PTSD-addled Vietnam vet in the Coens’ 1998 hardboiled slacker comedy qualifies as dangerous.)

“Adam is a fantastic, intense presence in [‘Paper Tiger’],” said Gray, who wrote “Paper Tiger” with Driver in mind.

Gray also spoke about the “recurring nightmares” for any filmmaker: “You screen your movie, and everybody walks out midway through. I’ve never had that happen to me, thank God.”

But one personal experience of watching this happen to someone else became seared in his unconscious: “When I was on the jury in Cannes [in 2009] … there was a movie made by a fantastic director. I won’t say his name, but he’s a great director of real reputation. And you have to sit in this jury box, which is sort of in the back of a theater, and the seats … when a person gets up, it’s spring-activated, and so it makes this very loud tack. I’m on the jury, and I’m watching this movie, and I start hearing tack, tack, tack, tack, tack, tack, tack. And people start walking out in droves. And the movie ended, and it was about half full, and people were booing. And that did become a nightmare for me. And by the way, I’m not the only director for whom that’s a nightmare. I’ve talked to many director friends of mine, and they’re like, ‘Oh, yeah. No, I’ve had that dream.'”

James Gray served on the Cannes jury in 2009 under president Isabelle Huppert — whom he reiterated, as Huppert previously did with IndieWire, he has no feud with despite rumors of a fractious deliberation — with such films as Gaspar Noé’s “Enter the Void” and Lars von Trier’s “Antichrist” in the competition. (But again, he’s not naming names here.)

“I know there’s directors who go, ‘I like it. I like when they boo,’ but that’s such a crock,” said Gray. We also asked for his thoughts on audiences dozing off in movies — which some directors, like Lucrecia Martel, have likened to falling asleep in the sun, a reflex of comfort — which certainly happens with some frequency at Cannes as any attendee knows.

“Who likes when you fall asleep during a movie? No, I’m sorry. The movie is required to keep you awake, and as Hitchcock once said, it has to be just long enough to accommodate your bladder’s capacity,” Gray said. “Which, by the way, you know when people say, ‘Oh, well, what do you think of the streaming thing and all that?’ I have only one real beef with streaming, and that’s the pause button, because it is my job to keep you there for an hour and a half, two hours, maybe even three. Where you’re not falling asleep, where you are riveted, where you’re not moving.”

He added, “I can’t stand the people who go, ‘I watched the first half on Tuesday, but I’m gonna catch the second half on a Saturday.’ … There’s nothing you can do about it, and it’s not, it’s not streamer-centered, because most people watch your films now at home. And whether it’s Netflix or Peacock or whatever, it doesn’t matter. The pause button is a problem.”

He pointed to his early relationship to “Vertigo,” a Hitchcock film he didn’t like in the first half, as an example of the virtues of experiencing a movie entirely in one sitting. “The result is so much more rewarding when you are forced to experience the whole thing because it’s like a dream, and you can’t pause your dream. And sometimes you don’t like your dream … sometimes the only way you can get yourself out of that dream is to convince yourself it is a dream in your dream. REM sleep is an hour and a half to two hours a night. What’s a movie’s runtime? It’s about the same thing. It didn’t happen by accident,” Gray said.

#3596. The Kindle Click Is the One Accessory Readers Have Been Waiting For

The Kindle is the world's most ubiquitous e-reader, but that's not the same as being the best. Don't get me wrong: Amazon deserves a large share of the credit for bringing e-books into the mainstream, and over the years, the Kindle has consistently offered a top-tier user experience, thanks to both generally good hardware and its integration into the retailer's ecosystem (for better or worse). But the company also rarely innovates in the space, waiting until other players like Barnes & Noble and Boox have tested out new features (like temperature-adjustable lighting and color screens, respectively) before adopting them itself. It's also not shy about dictating to customers what they can and can't do with their Kindles, from removing the ability to directly download copies of their e-books to limiting support for third-party accessories.

One such accessory has been maddeningly absent from the Kindle for years, despite the device having the technology in place to support it: a Bluetooth remote control (all Kindles released since 2018 support Bluetooth for connecting wireless headphones, but only wireless headphones).

A few years ago, third-party e-reader remotes became a big thing on BookTok, prompting competitors like Kobo and Boox to release their own versions of the peripherals. But with the Kindle's Bluetooth protocol locked down, Kindle owners were mostly out of luck; their only option a third-party clip-on accessory that attaches to the side of the device and manually taps the display at the press of a remote button—far from ideal, as they can only turn pages in one direction and block a portion of the screen.But finally, Amazon has seen the light and made its own Bluetooth remote, which it has dubbed the Kindle Click. More importantly, it has opened up the Bluetooth protocol within the Kindle firmware so it can connect to the accessory in the first place—though it will only work on Kindles from 2024 or later. (It pairs well with the new Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition, no pun intended.)

If you've never used one before, it can be a bit confusing to consider why someone would want a remote for their Kindle—why bother fussing with an extra device when you can just tap the screen or press a button? But for certain scenarios, it really does make sense.

Most practically, a remote can allow you to turn pages in circumstances where holding the e-reader itself is less than convenient, as when you're exercising: Holding a Kindle in your hands is tough when you're on an elliptical, and the words can bounce around too much if you're trying to use a spin bike while gulping down a few chapters of Yesteryear. But if you can prop the e-reader onto the machine's handlebars or a nearby surface, you can turn pages easily without missing a step.

Then there's the coziness factor: Reading under a big blanket in winter is one of the coziest activities I can imagine, but if you have to keep your arms outside of the blanket to turn pages on your Kindle, well, that's going to have an impact on how cozy you feel. (This is a real problem!) But what if you could comfortably arrange the device within your line of sight and turn pages while keeping your hands ensconced within your weighted throw? Some readers are willing to spend multiple tens of dollars to achieve this level of coziness.

How many dollars? In the case of the Kindle Click, around 35 of them (plus tax). Though that may seem like kind of a lot for a simple little remote with two basic functions and four buttons, it's just $5 more than the admittedly much cuter Boox Tappy. Speaking of which, while the new firmware update will also allow the Kindle to support cheaper third-party alternatives, there's no guarantee they will work as well.

So how does the Kindle Click work? Pretty seamlessly: You press and hold one button on the remote to put it in pairing mode. You open up the Settings menu on your 2024 or later Kindle and tap Accessories (you may need to perform a software update, if you aren't seeing that option). You tap Kindle Click in the resulting list to pair it. Once paired, the remote seems to connect to the Kindle automatically if the two devices are nearby and both powered up, provided you keep the latter's Bluetooth functionality turned on; you don't have to manually pair them every time.

That's pretty much it: Once you've opened a book, you can now turn pages with a button press (you can map which of the big grey buttons moves pages forward or back to suit your preferences). The volume-like buttons on the side can be used to adjust the brightness of the front light. You can't use the remote to navigate around the device or open a different book, so choose your reading material carefully before you enter your cocoon.

While the Click definitely works as advertised, Amazon could have been a bit more creative with its functionality. The Boox Tappy, for example, can switch between modes so it can be used to jump backward and forward between tracks in an audiobook or scroll pages in a web browser. While the Kindle can't display websites, it definitely supports audiobooks, but you can't use the Click to jump between chapters or adjust the volume while listening to an Audible book; these both seem like no-brainers to me.And while being able to turn the brightness up or down is nice, why not let the remote control the warmth settings as well, either through enabling different modes (like the Tappy) or via a combination of button presses? I'm not an engineer, so I don't know how complicated it would be to get that to work, but Amazon employs a lot of them, and I bet they could figure it out.

#3595. The Best Live-Action Sherlock Made The Biggest Change To Arthur Conan Doyle's Character

While there are countless screen versions of Arthur Conan Doyle’s iconic super sleuth, only the BBC’s iconic adaptation of Sherlock Holmes made the change that was needed to redefine the character for a new generation. Without Arthur Conan Doyle’s Sherlock Holmes, viewers would never have gotten the many cop shows and detective dramas that have filled TV listings and streaming services for decades now.

Everything from CBS’s NCIS franchise to True Detective, to Murder She Wrote, to Columbo, to the iconic small-town murder mystery Twin Peaks, all have their shared roots in the author’s iconic mystery stories. Sherlock Holmes was one of the first and most influential heroes of detective fiction, and Conan Doyle’s stories about the character provided many of the formative tropes that still define detective dramas, murder mysteries, and police procedurals to this day.

Despite this, many Sherlock Holmes adaptations have flopped over the decades. Even among the takes on the character that succeeded, almost none could be considered truly definitive takes on the character. While ABC’s Will Trent is the definitive screen version of Karin Slaughter’s novel hero, dozens of different takes on Holmes vie for supremacy. However, the BBC’s adaptation, Sherlock, has one major advantage over the rest of them.

In the past two years alone, Prime Video’s Young Sherlock, The CW’s Sherlock & Daughter, and CBS’s Watson have all, as their titles imply, attempted to find a fresh, original take on the familiar story of Sherlock Holmes. However, none of them have managed to replicate the magic of the BBC’s four-season, 13-episode Sherlock, a live-action version of the character from The League of Gentlemen’s Mark Gatiss and Doctor Who’s Steven Moffat.

Starring Benedict Cumberbatch as Sherlock himself and Martin Freeman as his long-suffering sidekick John Watson, Sherlock made the ingenious decision to move Conan Doyle’s original stories into a contemporary setting. This allowed Sherlock to reintroduce its iconic character as a louche antihero, and saw the BBC show regain some of the edge the original stories boasted during their publication.

While a lot of Sherlock Holmes adaptations lean into the cozy, twee familiarity of the character, much like many Agatha Christie murder mystery shows, it is worth noting that Conan Doyle’s Sherlock Holmes stories weren’t period pieces when they were originally published. The novels were fast-paced thrillers filled with what was then considered cutting edge science, meaning Sherlock’s modern-day setting is arguably truer to the books than a period setting would be.

There is no denying the reality that Sherlock’s final season dropped the proverbial ball and ensured the show didn’t achieve true greatness, but there was still a lot to love in the cult series. As well as making a star of Netflix’s future Tom Ripley, Andrew Scott, in a scene-stealing role as Moriarty, Sherlock provided an updated, thoroughly modern spin on a franchise that had become entirely too staid over the years.

In the years since Sherlock began, there have been innumerable efforts to revive the character for new audiences. 2012’s Elementary, 2018’s Miss Sherlock, the Netflix series The Irregulars, and the upcoming 2027 Sky production The Death of Sherlock Holmes all seek to offer new takes on one of the most iconic characters in literary history, and that’s without even mentioning the trio of hits shows listed above.

Clearly, for all of Sherlock’s flaws, the show’s decision to bring Sherlock into a modern-day setting undeniably injected new life into Conan Doyle’s creation. Imperfect final season or nine, the BBC’s Sherlock proved that Conan Doyle’s Baker Street sleuth was just as urgent and intriguing as ever provided the character got an overdue change of scenery and a new historical era to explore.
