#3594. 5 Sci-Fi Series To Watch If You Love HBO's 'Lanterns'

In brightest day, in blackest night, find your next binge watch tonight

HBO's Lanterns more than delivered when it comes to being both a great comic book series and a great piece of television. Not only did the series thrive thanks to the dynamic between Hal Jordan (Kyle Chandler) and John Stewart (Aaron Pierre), but it also managed to revitalize interest in the Green Lantern franchise following the less-than-stellar Green Lantern movie from 2011. That's a superhuman feat in and of itself, and Lanterns creators Damon Lindelof, Chris Mundy, and Tom King deserve credit for pulling that off.

While Pierre is slated to return as John Stewart in 2027's Man of Tomorrow, there are still plenty of other series that manage to feature sci-fi tropes and elements alongside a compelling mystery or two. Here are five that make for the perfect binge-watch.

Lanterns isn't the first time that Damon Lindelof has brought an iconic DC Comics series to life. In 2019, Lindelof served as the showrunner on Watchmen, an HBO series based on the legendary graphic novel by Alan Moore and Dave Gibbons. What makes Watchmen stand out is that it's fundamentally a sequel to the original comic, building on a world that was changed by the actions of Ozymandias (Jeremy Irons). Police officers are required to wear costumes after an attack by the Seventh Kalvary, a white supremacist group, made it necessary. One of these officers, Angela Abar (Regina King) — or "Sister Night", as she's known in costume — uncovers a mystery that ties to her family and one of Watchmen's key characters.

Much like Lanterns, Watchmen was met with mixed reception when it was first announced. Alan Moore's displeasure with adaptations of his work was well known at this point, and most fans asked why they should tune in when there was already a movie adaptation. However, Watchmen won over critics thanks to the way that it built on the original comic's events, while also weaving real history into its storytelling. It also weaves sci-fi elements into its narrative thanks to the presence of Doctor Manhattan, while still staying grounded. Fans looking for something that's similar to Lanterns definitely need to give Watchmen a look.

What makes Lanterns stand out from other superhero TV shows is that while it's part of DC Studios' creative slate, it feels tonally different from projects like Superman and Peacemaker. It's proof that a creator can enter a long-standing franchise and put their own creative stamp on it, and if fans are looking for a series that follows in the same spirit, they need to check out Andor. Taking place before the events of Rogue One: A Star Wars Story, Andor follows Cassian Andor (Diego Luna) as he gets swept up in the growing Rebellion. Cassian's growth from thief to revolutionary drives the story, as does the machinations of Luthen Rael (Stellan Skarsgard) and the struggles of Mon Mothma (Genevieve O'Reilly).

In the same way that Lanterns stands apart from the rest of DC Studios' work, Andor stands out from other Star Wars projects because it takes a hard look at the costs of rebellion. Cassian's journey sees him losing his mother and the love of his life, Bix Caleen (Adria Arjona); he's also imprisoned for months in an Imperial prison. Likewise, he bears witness to a horrifying genocide on the planet Ghorman as the Empire strips it for material for the Death Star. This approach, which comes courtesy of showrunnner Tony Gilroy, adds more depth to Rogue One and the Star Wars universe as a whole. It also shows that you can do so much more with Star Wars as a brand, which is a lesson more streamers should take with their established franchises.

Believe it or not, there was a time when Marvel and DC characters weren't dominating movie and television screens. True, there were shows like Smallville, but it appealed more to hardcore fans than new viewers. Things changed when Heroes made its debut in 2006 and took the world by storm. Heroes is unique in that while its characters did possess superhuman powers like being able to fly and stop time, they were normal people. Yet they start banding together to save the world from an impending apocalypse, leading to the now-iconic tagline: "Save the cheerleader, save the world."

Heroes did have a lengthy run of four seasons, but most fans agree that Season 1 is the zenith. It's when the show was firing on all cylinders, as its cast was full of future stars, including Zachary Quinto, and it managed to translate the larger-than-life elements that filled comic books to the small screen. Demand for fan-favorite characters derailed creator Tim Kring's plans to make Heroes into an anthology show, and the 2007 writers' strike cut Season 2 short. By the time Heroes returned, it was a shadow of its former self, but it was the first series to find humanity in superhumanity.

Streaming on: Pluto TV, Hulu, Prime Video

Anyone looking for sci-fi elements and a partnership like Lanterns should give Fringe a try. Fringe chronicles the journey of the Fringe Division, a secretive arm of the FBI that investigates cases related to a parallel universe. The Fringe Division consists of FBI Agent Olivia Dunham (Anna Torv), scientist Walter Bishop (John Noble), and Walter's son Peter (Joshua Jackson). As the series progresses, Fringe slowly ramps up its sci-fi elements, leading to some truly shocking reveals. None of them top the Season 1 finale "There's More Than One of Everything", which has one of the best final shots in TV history.

Long before multiverse stories were all the rage, Fringe tackled this concept head-on, and used it to explore questions of identity while also raising the series' stakes. The end result was the X-Files successor Fox had been looking for, and one of the rare sci-fi series that the network didn't cut down in its prime. Much like Heroes, Fringe also led to bigger things for its creators J.J. Abrams, Roberto Orci and Alex Kurtzman; the trio would reboot Star Trek for the silver screen, which reunited them with Leonard Nimoy.

Episodes available to purchase on Apple TV and YouTube

A decade ago, HBO launched its most ambitious attempt at a sci-fi series with Westworld. Inspired by the Michael Crichton movie of the same name, Westworld takes place in the far future, where the Delos Corporation has created a Western-themed amusement park full of lifelike androids that are willing to satisfy a wide range of appetites. Anyone who's watched The Terminator or any sci-fi story centering on artificial intelligence knows what happens next: the androids start to gain free will and eventually turn on humanity. What makes Westworld stand out from the pack is that it's built on a series of mysteries, including a "maze" within the park and the revelation that sentient "hosts" already exist.

Westworld was billed by many critics and fans as a worthy successor to Game of Thrones, though ironically, it wound up mirroring Heroes. After two stellar seasons, fans left in droves following Season 3, and Season 4 came and went with a whisper. On top of that, Westworld was one of the series that was axed in the "Great Purge" of HBO Max's library in 2022, meaning that fans will have to track down episodes digitally or buy the DVDs. Still, it helped pave the way for thought-provoking sci-fi, including Lanterns.

#3593. Emily Feingold Hired as EVP, Communications for The Walt Disney Company

Emily Feingold has been named Executive Vice President, Communications for The Walt Disney Company. She will begin her job next Monday.

Feingold is a veteran executive and is widely respected by the press as a straight shooter. She joins Disney after nearly nine years at Netflix, where she rose to become Vice President and Head of Communications for the U.S. and Canada. At the streaming giant, Feingold worked on corporate, financial, product and technology, advertising, content, marketing and consumer products communications. She advised senior leadership through some of Netflix’s biggest moments, including when co-founder Reed Hastings was succeeded as CEO by Ted Sarandos and Greg Peters. She also was in place when Netflix moved into advertising, live events, and gaming, as well as during its failed bid for Warner Bros. Discovery. Related Stories James Gray on His ‘Only Real Beef with Streaming’ and the ‘Recurring Nightmare’ That Started at Cannes in 2009 ‘I Play Rocky’ Celebrates Sylvester Stallone the Screenwriter — but Rocky Balboa Was Only the Beginning

Before Netflix, Feingold was Senior Vice President of Corporate Strategy and Communications at Andell Inc., a private investment firm, and Vice President of Corporate Communications at Ralph Lauren. She began her career at the White House.

At Disney, Feingold will report to Paul Roeder, Senior Executive Vice President and Chief Communications Officer, and oversee media relations, enterprise editorial, and executive, brand, financial and technology communications.

“Emily is one of the best in the business,” said Roeder. “She combines sharp instincts, broad experience and the trust and respect of colleagues and journalists alike. Jefferson is a former journalist who spent two decades reporting and editing for The Wall Street Journal and Newsweek. He will remain through the end of the month.

“David has been a trusted voice and steady hand for Disney through some of the most consequential moments in our history,” said Roeder. “I’ve known him since his days as a reporter, and I’m deeply grateful for his counsel, his friendship and everything he’s done for this company. I wish him every success in what comes next.”

#3592. 10 Hacks Every Fitbit Edge User Should Know

The Fitbit Edge really hits a sweet spot for anyone who wants a minimalist fitness tracker but still wants a screen to tell the time and display workout data. Here are my tips on how to get the most out of it, including hidden features and surprising ways to use the device.

It’s not very obvious from the watch or the app, but you can switch watch faces—and if you use the app on your phone, you can change color schemes and sometimes even complications.

On the watch, long-press the middle of the watch face. This brings up a carousel of the faces you’ve selected in the app. The last screen in the carousel gives you a button to bring up the watch face library on your phone. This is the quickest way to open it, but you can also go to your device settings in the app.

From here, tap All Clocks and browse the available faces. Once you’ve installed a face you like, tap Customize to choose a color scheme and select which complications appear (like your steps for the day, or the weather). Sadly, the share button doesn’t seem to work—it sends a broken link to the old Fitbit website—but it’s a nice idea.

The Fitbit Edge is built with the assumption that you’ll want the side button on the right. But if you wear other jewelry or watches with it, or if you wear it low on your wrist and find that flexing your hand pushes the button, you can change this.

Just go into your device settings in the Google Health app, tap Device preferences, and then change Tracker orientation to put the button on the left instead of the right. This turns the display upside down, so take off your watch and turn it around so you can see it properly again.

The AI-powered Health Coach is both the best and the worst thing about the Google Health app. Fortunately, you can turn it off. What’s better, Google added a feature that lets you turn off the unprompted insights while still having the AI available when you need it.

Tap your profile picture in the app, then Google Health Settings, then Coaching, and select No Coach Insights. The chatty summaries (and notifications) will stop popping up throughout the day, but you can always hit the Ask Coach button if you have a question or if you want to use AI-powered food logging or workout logging.

The workout app on the Fitbit Edge is pretty minimal and can’t be customized, but it is possible to get more information during your workouts. Swipe down from the top of your Fitbit Edge screen, and tap the icon that looks like a wifi heart. This turns on heart-rate broadcasting.

Then go into the Strava app, hit Record to start a workout, and swipe up from the bottom of the screen to see workout options. Select the Fitbit Edge as your heart rate sensor, and now your phone can track your workout using heart rate data from the Fitbit. The Strava app gives you a lap button and can show you the time for your previous laps; it also shows you a map of where you are and where you’ve been.

Fitbit devices have always been a little over-enthusiastic about counting steps compared to other wearables, and they know it. Hand and arm movements can mistakenly contribute to your step count, but there’s a way to adjust the device’s sensitivity. If you wear the device on your dominant hand (say, on your right hand if you’re right-handed), go into Device preferences on the phone app and set your Wrist preference to dominant.

If you already wear the device on your non-dominant hand, you may still want to use this hack. Wear it on your left hand (if you’re right-handed) and still change your preference to dominant. This will tell the Fitbit to slightly undercount your steps.

The Fitbit Edge can use its own built-in GPS, or it can use the GPS that is built into your phone. By default, it will switch sources automatically based on what it thinks the best option will be.

But you can change this. Go into Device preferences again, and choose GPS settings. If you always carry your phone with you, and you’d prefer to save battery on your Fitbit, tell the device to always use your phone's GPS. On the other hand, if you want the Fitbit to handle its own GPS without piggybacking on your phone all the time, tell it to use the built-in GPS instead.

If your phone is an older one, switching to the built-in GPS will probably give you more accurate distance and pace than using the default switching. If your phone is newer, choose based on which device you want to preserve battery.

At the same time as the Fitbit Edge came out, Google made it so that the app can work with multiple Fitbits. If you sometimes like to have a screen on your wrist, but sometimes you don’t, you can swap seamlessly back and forth between the Edge and the Air (and a Pixel watch, should you happen to have one of those as well). No extra steps are necessary—just set up both of them, and wear whichever you feel like at any given moment.

Small screens can mean less visibility, but there is a setting that helps. In Device preferences, select Magnification and toggle it on. Now, triple-tapping the screen (three quick taps with one finger) enlarges what you’re looking at. You can use your finger to move the image around the screen to see different parts—for example, to get a better look at the number under the step count complication on some watch faces.

In this part of the app, you can also choose whether the magnification gesture gives you a 2x or a 3x zoom. To zoom out, just triple-tap the screen again.

The charger for the Fitbit Edge (like that for the Pixel Watch) is incredibly fast. If your watch is running low on charge and you don't have time to wait for it to charge, just put it on the charger for five minutes. Google says this gives it enough juice for a full day, and that matches my experience. Just now, three minutes of charging brought the device from 31% up to 41%.

If your Fitbit Edge tends to last about a week, you'll need about 15% to get through a full day. I like to use the always-on display (AOD), so I only get about three days per charge. If you're using the five-minute trick because you're low on battery, turn off the AOD if you have it enabled, and you'll get through the rest of the day. But if you always have the AOD enabled, you may be able to get into the habit of charging your Fitbit for about five minutes every day—maybe 10 every now and then—and never have to walk away from it for an hour like you would with most wearables.

I don’t follow the workouts the AI coach gives me, but it can be nice to have a record of what I did. So I’ll take a screenshot of my workout in Hevy, or a photo of my training journal, and show it to the Coach.

You can do this from the Ask Coach button in the bottom right corner of the app. Tell it which workout it should attach the exercises to (for example, “log this for my strength training session from last night”), and it will fill in the exercises in that workout summary. You can view past workouts in the Fitness tab.

#3591. 10 Essential K-Drama Shows That Belong on Every Fan's Bucket List

There’s no shortage of K-dramas to watch, but choosing what to put on next can be an arduous task. With stories spanning everything from slow-burn romances to coming-of-age dramas, K-dramas have something for everyone. No longer limited by geographical boundaries, the genre has also gained considerable popularity in Western markets.

This growing global audience has encouraged K-dramas to experiment with Western influences, expanding beyond traditional melodramas into thrillers, crime dramas, and more. Of course, some shows have become fan favorites and frequently pop up in recommendations. From one of Netflix’s most popular hits to series starring some of South Korea’s biggest stars, these are essential K-drama shows that belong on every fan’s bucket list.

If there's one K-drama that takes the biggest risk in reimagining North-South Korean relations, it's Crash Landing on You. The series follows heiress Yoon Se Ri (Son Ye Jin), whose paragliding accident lands her in North Korea, where she meets army captain Ri Jeong Hyeok (Hyun Bin).

Escaping North Korea is part of the plot, but the hook is watching Se Ri build relationships with people from a different world. From her friendship with the North Korean village women to Jeong Hyeok's fellow soldiers, the K-drama shows that people are alike, regardless of how their governments portray them. Despite its inaccuracies, the series finds common ground across a politically divided country.

With debts piling up and no way to pay them off, Seong Gi-hun (Lee Jung-jae) takes a chance on a mysterious competition offering a life-changing cash prize. He joins 455 other players in a series of childhood games, including Red Light, Green Light and the dalgona challenge. There's just one catch: anyone who loses is shot dead, while the prize money keeps growing with every eliminated contestant.

Fans can't talk about K-drama masterpieces without bringing up Squid Game, especially after the grip it had on global audiences. The death game TV series takes something as innocent as childhood playground games and turns it into a disturbing look at capitalism, class inequality, and the lengths people will go to when they're desperate for money.

Revenge takes on a whole different meaning in The World of the Married, where Ji Seon-u (Kim Hee-ae) refuses to let her cheating husband walk away without consequences. After discovering Lee Tae-oh's (Park Hae-joon) affair with Yeo Da-kyung (Han So-hee), Seon-u turns their divorce into a cold, calculated attempt to dismantle the life he built behind her back.

If there's one revenge K-drama that makes you want to see a cheater get what they deserve, it's this one. From inviting her husband's mistress to dinner to quietly securing his assets before the divorce, Seon-u's moves are deeply satisfying to watch. But her obsession with revenge also puts her family through the wringer, making the fallout just as gut-wrenching.

Kirin High is where six aspiring performers come to prove they have what it takes to become K-pop stars. Coming from different backgrounds, from wealthy students with industry connections to newcomers from the countryside, they all share the same dream of making it in music. But talent alone won't get them there, especially when everyone is fighting for the same spotlight.

With K-pop's global popularity, Dream High is worth watching for its look at the pressures of idol training and how privilege can shape someone's chances of making it. Not everyone plans to be a star, but the students' grit to pursue music despite their circumstances makes this coming-of-age K-drama all the more relatable. Featuring the biggest K-pop stars like Bae Suzy and IU, expect stellar performances along the way.

Joon-sang (Bae Yong-jun) and Yoo-jin (Choi Ji-woo) are high school students from different backgrounds who fall in love. Just as their relationship begins to blossom, Joon-sang gets into a devastating accident that leaves him with no memory of his past. Presumed dead, he eventually resurfaces a decade later, but without any recollection of the life he once shared with Yoo-jin.

The ultimate K-drama of the turn of the millennium, Winter Sonata delivers an emotional roller coaster through Joon-sang's struggle to recover his memories. While his survival brings relief, watching him slowly uncover the past he shared with Yoo-jin is heartbreaking, especially as each revelation brings back painful memories.

Four of the largest communities on the planet, and four completely different reasons to belong to one. Here is yours, what it would give you, and the argument you would be having within a week.

You belong to the fandom that is really about comfort. Hogwarts works on people because it is a place rather than a plot, and the pull is not the wizard war so much as the corridors, the food, the weather and the sense that somebody is expecting you.

You belong to the deepest fandom on this list, the one where somebody has always read further than you and is quietly delighted to say so. Middle-earth rewards patience more than any other world in popular culture.

You belong to the loudest and largest tent of the four, the one where three generations are all watching the same thing and none of them agree about any of it. That disagreement is not a flaw in this fandom, it is the main activity.

You belong to the thinking fandom, the one that turns up for the argument rather than the explosion. Trek has always been a series of ethical problems in space, and the people who love it love being asked what they would have done.

Childhood friends Eun-su (Jeon So-nee) and Hui-su (Lee You-mi) live very different lives. Eun-su works in retail, selling “apology jewelry” to people looking to make amends, while Hui-su is trapped in an abusive marriage. When Eun-su learns what her friend has been going through, she refuses to keep watching from the sidelines.

As You Stood By questions people who witness abuse but choose to stay out of it, allowing abusers to carry on without consequence. After everyone else fails to step in, Eun-su and Hui-su decide to take matters into their own hands. Their actions in this recent K-drama hit may come from a desire to protect Hui-su, but that doesn't spare either woman from having to face what they've done.

Park Tae-jung (Ji Chang-wook) never expects a simple act of kindness to turn his life upside down. After returning a lost phone, the food delivery driver becomes the prime suspect in a murder. His time in prison takes an even darker turn when he meets another inmate who was also set up under similar circumstances. With nothing left to lose, Tae-jung decides to fight back.

The Manipulated hits uncomfortably close to home. In an age when personal information is constantly collected and shared, even the smallest details can become weapons in the wrong hands. A name, a photograph, or a leaked piece of data can be twisted to destroy someone's life, particularly when those targeted have little power to defend themselves.

Boys Over Flowers is the K-drama of the late 2000s. The story begins when Geum Jan-di (Koo Hye-sun), a working-class girl, receives a scholarship to the prestigious Shinhwa High School after preventing a student from taking his own life. Her sudden arrival puts her on the radar of F4, a clique of four of the most popular boys at school.

Boys Over Flowers is practically a time capsule of the tropes that would come to define modern K-dramas: the familiar rich-boy-meets-poor-girl formula, complete with antagonistic beginnings, extravagant love triangles, and plenty of melodramatic twists. The series rarely does anything halfway, but that's part of its appeal.

Set on 1950s Jeju Island, When Life Gives You Tangerines follows two childhood sweethearts from very different worlds. Ae-sun (IU) is a headstrong dreamer with a passion for poetry, while Gwan-sik (Park Bo-gum) is a quiet, pragmatic young man who struggles to express his feelings. Despite their differences, they find comfort in each other.

Spanning seven decades, the series explores love through life's joys and cruelties. Ae-sun and Gwan-sik's youthfulness brings warmth, but their upbringing is marked by a turbulent period in Korean history. As the years pass, their story becomes a reminder that loving someone also means learning to live with the pain of eventually losing them.

When a mysterious plague begins spreading across Joseon Korea, Crown Prince Lee Chang (Ju Ji-hoon) grows suspicious of the circumstances surrounding his father's sudden seclusion. His investigation leads to a shocking discovery: the dead are coming back to life, threatening the empire from within.

A Korean historical drama built around a zombie outbreak may sound like an unlikely combination, but Kingdom pulls it off. Its action scenes are brutal and leave nobody spared from being eaten. But the undead aren't Lee Chang's only problem. While he tries to contain the outbreak, powerful figures at court are busy fighting over the throne, leaving the kingdom vulnerable from both within and beyond its walls.

#3590. Magic: The Gathering Star Trek Perfectly Captures the Sci-Fi Show’s Most Brutal Running Joke

Generating creature tokens is a common way to make the most out of your resources in a game of Magic: The Gathering. They can be sacrificed for powerful effects, used to chump block, or amassed to overwhelm your opponent. Cards typically generate tokens of the same color, like white Warriors for Secure the Wastes, green Squirrels for Deranged Hermit, and black Zombies for Ghoulish Procession. Yet numerous cards in Magic: The Gathering Star Trek generate 1/1 red Officer tokens regardless of the base color, from the white Captain Benjamin Sisko to the green MACO Strike Team. The discrepancy is a nod to the sci-fi franchise’s darkest running joke.

Star Trek: The Original Series established that Starfleet officers wear brightly colored uniforms based on their job. Captain James T. Kirk sports gold to indicate he’s in command. Spock and Dr. Leonard McCoy wear blue, the color of Starfleet’s medical and science divisions. Red is the color of security and operations, worn by chief engineer Montgomery Scott and communications officer Nyota Uhura.

The series follows the U.S.S. Enterprise on a five-year mission to explore strange new worlds and seek out new life and new civilizations. When the ship finds a planet to investigate, they typically send down a few members of the senior staff along with some extra security and operations personnel for support. The show’s writers tended to kill off these nameless red-clad officers to show the situation was serious without hurting one of the show’s main characters. These disposable background characters came to be referred to as redshirts. You can see one such moment in the art for the removal spell He’s Dead, Jim, which shows McCoy bending over a redshirt who died on an alien planet, delivering the bad news to Captain Kirk.

Star Trek: The Next Generation actually changed the color of uniforms so that red was worn by the ship’s top officers, Captain Jean-Luc Picard and Commander William T. Riker. The show also found a new way of proving the situation was serious: beating up Chief Security Officer Worf. But the name for the trope was already so well established that it stuck.

John Scalzi wrote a Hugo Award-winning novel called Redshirts that follows an ensign on a starship where the crew is terrified of going on away missions or even being around the ship’s senior officers because of their disturbingly high casualty rate. In the Star Trek parody Galaxy Quest, Guy Fleegman (Sam Rockwell) played a nameless character in a single episode of the show who was quickly killed off. When alien fans of the series abduct the show’s cast, Guy is convinced that he’s going to experience the same fate as his character. But he survives the adventure and winds up getting elevated to Security Chief for the show’s reboot.

The red Officer tokens generated by Magic Star Trek cards perfectly represent the redshirt trope. They are disposable creatures you can use to block or sacrifice to cards like General Chang, Cold Warrior while protecting your more important cards. They’re especially likely to die to the Borg, who generate their own 1/1 creature tokens. But the Officers can also be used to Station Spacecraft and even allow a player to search their deck for a Spacecraft to put onto the battlefield with the help of Captain Jean-Luc Picard.

Magic’s Universes Beyond sets can have a hard time sorting existing characters and ideas into the mechanics of Magic’s five colors. Magic Star Trek divides characters based on their personalities rather than uniform color, though there are some times that they align like Will Riker, First in the Field and Mr. Spock, Science Officer. Creating 1/1 Officer tokens would most commonly be a white effect, like generating 1/1 white Soldiers with Resolute Reinforcements or 1/1 white Monks with Monastery Mentor. But the set’s designers clearly made the disposable Starfleet members red as a nod to the show’s most enduring dark trope.

#3589. Box Office: ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Roars with $6.7 Million in Previews, ‘Ramayana: Rise of a Legend’ Earns $3.5 Million

#3588. 10 Hacks Every iCloud User Should Know

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

If you accidentally delete or overwrite a file or contact that's synced to iCloud, you can restore it from the Recovery portal on iCloud.com. This feature works across many Apple apps, including Calendar, Contacts, Mail, Photos, Notes, and Reminders, as well as Drive, Pages, Numbers, and Keynote. When you restore an old version of your data, the current version is archived so you can revert back if you change your mind. Deleted files can be recovered within 30 days.

One benefit of an iCloud+ subscription is Apple's Hide My Email, which allows you to create unique, random aliases to keep your real email address private. These addresses forward to your primary inbox, and replies appear to come from the alias rather than your personal email. There's no limit on how many Hide My Email addresses you can generate, so you can use them for newsletter sign-ups, online shopping, and any other credential you may want to deactivate if you start getting spammed. Hide My Email is compatible with Safari, Mail, Apple Pay, and some third-party apps.

Apple supports legacy contacts for Apple Accounts, meaning you can designate someone to receive access to your data—including photos, files, messages, and backups—after your death. This allows you to use iCloud as a digital vault for storing documents and other important information that can be securely passed down. (Note that legacy contacts will not receive iCloud Keychain data like passwords and passkeys, so you'll need another way to share this information if desired.) To designate a legacy contact, go to Settings > [Your Name] > Sign-In & Security > Legacy Contact and follow the prompts. That person will need the access key you generate and your death certificate to take over your accounts.

Apple's Family Sharing allows up to six users to share a single iCloud+ subscription while maintaining separate Apple Accounts. This means that each user has their own private vault for photos, documents, and backups while gaining access to premium features and a lot more storage overall. iCloud+ offers plans from 50 GB to 12 TB of storage. Family Sharing likely makes the most sense if you can fill most or all of the seats and/or already pay for or plan to use close to the limit of one of the higher-cost plans (compared to each individual paying for their own subscription).

Sorting through photos and adding them to a shared album after a vacation can feel like a huge project—but iCloud can do this work for you in real time if your friends and family have iPhones with Bluetooth enabled and are logged into their Apple Accounts. Set up an iCloud Shared Photo Library in the Photos app under Collections > [Your account] > Shared Library and add up to five participants. Then, from Shared Library, tap Sharing from Camera > Share Automatically. If you take photos when other album participants are nearby, they will be uploaded to the shared album.

If you want to text a large photo or video to someone who doesn't have an Apple Account and access to iCloud photos without compressing the file, you can create a temporary link that gives them access to view and download the file for 30 days. This also allows you to share multiple files with a single link rather than sending them individually, and you can revoke access whenever you'd like. To create an iCloud link, open an image, tap Share, and select Copy iCloud Link.

Note that as of iOS 27 and macOS 27, Apple now supports adding Windows and Android users to iCloud Shared Albums. However, temporary links are still a good solution if you don't want to share whole albums.

iCloud's backup feature will automatically back up your iPhone periodically so you can restore your data if your device is lost or stolen. This includes information that isn't regularly synced to iCloud storage, like settings and app organization. You can disable cellular backups to restrict backups to wifi only—or you can turn on low data mode, which will allow for backing up over your cellular connection except when speeds are low, or your data is capped. Low data mode could also save battery by not straining a slow connection. You can enable low data mode for cellular via Settings > Cellular > Cellular Data Options > Data Mode.

If your Apple device is backing up to iCloud, you could regularly bump up against your storage limit, especially if you aren't paying for a large amount of space. One way to mitigate this is to cut down what gets backed up, which you can do at the app level. If you have apps you don't use regularly or don't need data from, you can disable them from your iCloud backups. Go to your Apple account in the Settings app and tap iCloud > Storage > Backups > [This iPhone] to manage app backups.

If you sync tons of photos and files to iCloud along with device backups, you may find yourself hitting the storage cap. But you don't necessarily have to buy more storage space, nor are you stuck manually deleting items one by one. Instead, go to Settings > [Your Account] > iCloud > Recommended For You to find suggestions for freeing up storage space. This may include deleting inactive backups or reviewing your files or photos and videos, which are categorized by duplicates, screenshots, and videos (the content you're most likely to be able to offload). If you don't see these options under Recommended For You, go back to iCloud > Storage and select the app you want to clean up. Finally, check what's included in your device backups, and disable any apps you don't need under iCloud > Storage > Backups.

#3587. Legend Of Zelda: Ocarina Of Time Remake Official DLC Incoming

At the time of writing, The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake is finally out on the Nintendo Switch 2, and what a journey it has been. First launching back in 1998 for the Nintendo 64, it was the first entry in the beloved Nintendo franchise to offer players 3D graphics and now, after almost three decades, it is still considered one of the greatest video games of all time.

Despite receiving a remake back in 2011 for the Nintendo 3DS, fans have been calling out for a modern-day Switch remake for the past few years, and it was earlier this year, amidst celebrations for The Legend of Zelda's 40th anniversary, that Nintendo announced that The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake would be arriving on 5 November.

Now a few days on from that launch, and there are still more exciting releases to come, as the beloved remake is set to receive official DLC.

It was ahead of the launch of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake that Nintendo revealed amiibo support for the game. Each with their own exclusive unlocks, players will be able to access Young Link and Young Zelda when they arrive and, by using the accompanying code, will be able to add them to their game. The confusion here is that these amiibo are set to launch in 2027 rather than alongside the game.

It has not yet been revealed when in 2027 they will be released, but we can only hope that it is in the first few months, so that people are still playing through The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake. Alternatively, more amiibo inspired by the game could be in the pipeline, and perhaps launching slightly earlier.

Using the amiibo in the game will see Link and Zelda put on masks inspired by their younger looks. It is currently unclear if these masks will serve any purpose, or if they are simply decorational and a nod to their previous iterations. Nevertheless, it is cool to see how far the beloved gaming pair have come, and that is not to mention the improvement in graphics.

There are also a few more mysteries surrounding these upcoming amiibo releases. How will they be transferable to the game? Can they be scanned in exchange for rewards in-game? Not only that, but we have next to no idea when exactly they will launch, how much they will be, and if they are able to be pre-ordered ahead of time.

For now, we have more questions than answers, but there is no denying that these brand-new Link and Zelda Ocarina of Time Remake-inspired amiibo are pretty adorable, so we can only hope that they can be used for more than just decoration. That being said, if they are anything like previous amiibo released for titles such as The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild and The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom, then using them could see the player earn repeatable resources such as money and ammo.

#3586. The Johnny Depp Comeback Hits Judgment Day with ‘Ebenezer’: How Paramount Is Carefully Reintroducing the Controversial Star

Hollywood studios turned away Johnny Depp eight years ago. With “Ebenezer,” Paramount Pictures is betting that audiences have not rejected him too. The “A Christmas Carol” adaptation, out November 13, marks a decisive moment for the studio, as it was one of the first films boarded by the company after its 2025 acquisition by Skydance.

Depp got some positive social media attention Monday evening when he was filmed “wyling out” and “wreaking havoc” in the Christmas Market of New York’s Bryant Park — as Scrooge, of course. In his first major pre-release promotional stop for “Ebenezer,” Depp donned a fright wig and make-up to enact some staged bah-humbugging, which included popping balloons, knocking over a Christmas tree, and playfully antagonizing an on-site Santa Claus. The stunt was Depp’s second in-character appearance as Scrooge, coming three months after a similarly interactive appearance at San Diego Comic-Con that also generated mounds of social media content from passerby. Later on at the event, Scrooge appeared onstage during Collider’s Directors on Directing panel to debut the first “Ebenezer” trailer. Related Stories Ebenezer’s Venmo and ‘How to Rob a Bank’ ATMs: Studios Are Now Promoting Movies by Just Giving Away Money The Bay Theater in Palisades Village, Closed Since the LA Wildfires, Will Reopen Thanks to Paramount and Rick Caruso

The approach leans into how audiences know Depp, who became one of the industry’s biggest stars in the aughts with his quirked-up performances in the “Pirates of the Caribbean” franchise and various Tim Burton joints. But several publicity veterans note that it’s also a strategy that helps the star skirt addressing himself: a typical component to the modern promotional gauntlet of podcast appearances and junketing. Paramount and representatives for Depp declined to comment for this story.

Indeed, the last time Depp was promoting a blockbuster in character was at Warner Bros.’ San Diego Comic-Con panel in 2018, where he appeared as Gellert Grindelwald, the seductively authoritarian wizard within J.K. Rowling’s world of “Harry Potter,” to promote the second “Fantastic Beasts” prequel. Depp was mired in controversy at the time, as his ex-wife, Amber Heard, alleged that he had been “physically abusive” in court documents filed in their divorce case. Depp denied the claims. Making things more awkward — Heard appeared at the same studio presentation, popping up an hour later for a panel hyping “Aquaman.”

Two years later, Depp departed from a third (and what ended up to be the final) “Fantastic Beasts” entry. On Instagram, the actor posted that he had been “asked to resign” by the studio. Depp had just lost a U.K. libel trial against The Sun, in which a judge ruled that an article reporting that the actor was a “wife beater” was found to be “substantially true.”

But Depp later claimed victory in a U.S. defamation trial against Heard herself. Heard had written a Washington Post op-ed in which she described herself as a survivor of domestic abuse. Depp claimed the article damaged his reputation and career; both parties argued the other was the aggressor through the grueling six-week spectacle. An initial jury ruling sided with Depp on three separate claims of defamation, ordering Heard pay him $10.35 million in damages. Heard won on one of her three counterclaims of defamation, ordering Depp to pay her $2 million. A later appeal by Heard ended with a settlement in which she agreed to pay $1 million to Depp.

The highly-gawked-at and internet-scrutinized trial reignited his fame and infamy, depending on your perspective. Once a big-screen titan, he was now ubiquitous on social media, particularly TikTok, emerging with an ardent online fanbase forged by a conviction that he was a man who had been rashly cast aside during the #MeToo movement’s prominence in the late 2010’s.

With “Ebenezer,” Paramount has the unique assignment of capitalizing on that celebrity, without inviting relitigation of an ugly legal battle that would cloud the sunny promotion of a family feature. Hence, the in-character appearances, along with underlining Depp’s penchant for transformative turns (though no further ones are planned). A promotional video featuring snippets of cast interviews, including the likes of Ian McKellen, Daisy Ridley, and Tramell Tillman, praise the actor as giving “a performance the likes of which you’ve never seen before.”

“A less clever route would be turning the release into a ‘comeback’ victory lap. The result could be an unnecessary and noisy polarization of views, reviving the very controversy the studio would prefer to move beyond,” says media lawyer and crisis manager Amber Melville-Brown, who heads the media and reputation team at the law firm Withers. “A campaign built around vindication invites an argument about who, precisely, has been vindicated and for what — starting the debate over again. A campaign built around the performance sparks a different conversation.”

Meanwhile, Paramount has been careful to show “Ebenezer” to select audiences so far. The film was unveiled Sunday in New York City with a “special screening” at the Whitby Hotel’s 147-seat screening room — an intimate venue for the first unveiling of a studio feature. A handful of press outlets and more influencers were invited to a small carpet. One front-facing video posted by a guest featured her meeting Depp and calling the occasion “my sign from God that I chose the right path today.” A London premiere will take place at Odeon Luxe Leicester Square on Monday.

In another shrewd booking, Depp made a surprise onstage appearance during Aerosmith’s Hollywood Bowl concert on October 29. While other actors may tap in for a late-night spot or “Hot Ones” interview to mark the home stretch of film promotion, Depp instead let a guitar solo on “Train Kept A-Rollin'” do the talking.

Down the line, the “Ebenezer” review embargo will lift November 12, mere hours before public screenings begin — almost always a sign that a studio has little confidence in finding good PR from the critic class. The film’s director, Ti West, has usually drawn positive reviews through his career, mostly known as an indie horror darling until this first studio feature.

But most importantly for Paramount, “Ebenezer” doesn’t need to be a blockbuster to find success. The film’s production budget netted out to a rather modest $38 million, giving it a much easier pathway to theatrical profitability than Depp’s previous mega-budget tentpoles. Along with that comes hopes to leg out through the holiday season and a bank on grosses from overseas territories, where other older male movie stars like Brad Pitt and Tom Cruise have better retained their ability to sell tickets.

Rival studios are looking closely at whether audiences still see Depp as a big screen draw. Lionsgate is already in the Depp business for the revenge thriller “Day Drinker,” releasing in March. And at Disney’s D23 Expo in August, “Pirates of the Caribbean” producer Jerry Bruckheimer floated hopes to get the star on board for a sixth installment. That franchise has laid dormant for nearly a decade, despite numerous reports of development teams tinkering on a Depp-less take. In one of the more interesting quotes from the “Ebenezer” event in New York, Depp spoke with Entertainment Tonight and slid in a dig at the 2017 entry “Dead Men Tell No Tales,” saying he’d be open to a franchise return but noting that “the only involvement I really want to have, truly, is just to send them off on a better note.”

But when Depp was first jettisoned from Hollywood’s A-list, major studios had begun to tire of his antics. There were reports of erratic on-set behavior, sky-high salary demands, and — in the true offender for studios — diminishing box office returns. The “Pirates” films still made money, but Depp headlined several costly bombs, including “Alice Through the Looking Glass” and “Mortdecai,” which had left companies less eager to write big checks, particularly given his public relations scandals.

But Depp’s absence may have not curbed his following. A National Research Group study from earlier this year found that he was the seventh-most cited name by people, especially in Europe, when they wre asked to name five actors or actresses that would motivate them to see “a new movie in a cinema,” even though he’s been away from the big screen for nearly a decade. Over those years, a growing refrain in the business has been that some movie stars have kneecapped their ability to open films by signing on to streaming productions, curbing consumers’ association of them with theaters. In that context, Depp may prove to be a unicorn, having essentially sat out years of the industry chasing Netflix — even if it wasn’t his choice to.

#3585. 'The Matrix's Best Line Is Still the Greatest Quote in Franchise History

Though there are many great sci-fi quotes that have been influential in how we view the genre, one line in The Wachowskis’ seminal blockbuster The Matrix has left the biggest mark. The 1999 classic changed the game for how we look at cinema effects, but this line, delivered by Laurence Fishburne to Keanu Reeves, also shows how the movie changed our perception of storytelling. While the film coined some famous phrases that are used to this day, the one that had the most impact is probably the least celebrated.

The line in question comes when Thomas Anderson, aka Neo (Reeves), is retrieved by Trinity (Carrie-Anne Moss) and brought to her leader, Morpheus (Fishburne). Neo sits down with Morpheus, and the latter begins explaining why they are here—because Neo feels a greater truth that he can’t explain, something wrong with the world that feels like “a splinter in your mind.” That feeling can be summed up as “The Matrix,” something that Morpheus describes as a prison that all human beings are born into.

He then leans back with a small case in his hand, and says: “Unfortunately, no one can be told what The Matrix is. You have to see for yourself.” He then offers Neo the famous option of the red and blue pills. Choosing red frees him from The Matrix and awakens him to his reality. Choosing blue allows him to carry on living in the illusion. There are many great lines in movie, but this is perhaps the most impactful, as it defines the nature of the journey all of us are about to take.

It might seem like today, you can find out everything you need to know about a movie from a quick internet search. Trailers, scenes, even the first 10 minutes of a release are routinely shared as part of the marketing. The Matrix was different, with marketing being kept purposefully vague in terms of the storyline to pique viewers’ interest. The infamous first teaser trailer for the film showed a series of unconnected clips without an explanation of the plot, before inviting people to visit www.whatisthematrix.com to gather more clues.

It was a ploy that worked, but even those who ventured into theaters absolutely knowing what The Matrix is were told by this line that it is better to experience it than intellectualize it. On the surface, Morpheus absolutely tells Neo what The Matrix is before saying, “You have to see it for yourself.” The point of the line is that his experience as a character, and ours as a viewer, is better when we see the explanation unfold in front of our eyes. The Matrix is experienced, not debated. It’s lived, not relayed.

The Wachowskis’ work has stood the test of time over a quarter of a century later, and the proof of that influence is in the lines from the movie that have made it into everyday language. The term “red pilled” has made its way into online discourse, while lines such as “free your mind” and “dodge this” have been quoted by fans of the movies ever since. However, Morpheus’ enigmatic quote has the biggest impact, as it sets the viewer up for an experience that, up to that point, was unlike anything else that had been seen in mainstream cinema.

From that moment, we were encouraged to take Neo’s point of view, and leave ourselves open to the adventures of The Matrix. Taking the red pill in that regard meant diving into a timeless spectacle of kung fu, post-apocalyptic sci-fi, and self-liberation. Accepting what came along allowed you to gasp as Neo dodged bullets, leaped from buildings, and defied gravity in one of the greatest climactic fights in cinema history.

There were many imitators that came after The Matrix, films that used the same aesthetics, concepts, and choreography to mimic the pioneering spirit of that 1999 film. However, the original inspiration worked because it refused to be defined by what came before it. The Matrix, both as a concept and as a film, can be written down or explained, but as Morpheus so rightly said, the best way to find out is to see it for yourself.

The 65-inch LG Evo C6 OLED TV has dropped to $1,399.99 from $1,599.99, a $200 price cut that brings it to its lowest price ever, according to price trackers—and the savings aren't limited to this particular size either, with discounts extending across the C6 lineup, from the compact 42-inch model to the massive 83-inch version, although the 65-inch screen is particularly appealing if you want a larger OLED without spending more than $1,500. The nearly bezel-free design also keeps the focus on the picture, while its 4K OLED panel delivers bright HDR highlights in Dolby Vision, HDR10, and HLG content. #3583. Sydney Sweeney's New Netflix Sci-Fi Epic Is Mandatory Viewing For Transformers Fans

Transformers is a franchise that has built-in appeal in more ways than one. Apart from the concept of giant robots transforming into vehicles, there's the fact that two factions of these robots have been engaged in a war that spans millenia. There have been highs (including the grossly underrated Transformers One) and lows (including most of Michael Bay's films), but it's more than likely that we'll be seeing Transformers stories until the heat death of the universe. Netflix is aiming to deliver its own take on another property that features giant robots, and it's tapped Sydney Sweeney to play a leading role in this potential franchise.

That series is none other than Mobile Suit Gundam. Like Transformers, the Gundam franchise has had multiple installments over the decades, and zeroes in on a conflict between two opposing factions, with each of them piloting the massive "mobile suits" that are Gundam's namesake. Sweeney leads a star-studded cast that includes Noah Centineo (Street Fighter), Jason Isaacs (Harry Potter), and Michael Mando (Spider-Man: No Way Home), with Jim Mickle serving as writer and director. Mickle's no stranger to adapting genre fare for Netflix, as he previously gave the streamer one of its best series with Sweet Tooth. Gundam might pose a different challenge.

While most people watch a Gundam series and see giant robots fighting in outer space, its creator had much deeper themes in mind. Tomino Yoshiyuki has been fairly open about how growing up in the thick of World War II shaped his approach to Mobile Suit Gundam, and how 'he realized the only reason to build a giant mobile suit was to use it for war. Kenji Kamiyama, who's working on the upcoming Mobile Suit Gundam RG: XARX-ZERO, beautifully summed up why Gundam continues to thrive.

“Mobile suits themselves are weapons of war. So how have humans evolved their way of fighting through that?"

That's a question that Netflix's take on Gundam should answer, and for a time, it looked like that was going to happen. Jordan Vogt-Roberts and Brian K. Vaughn were originally attached to the project; both men previously helmed projects that dealt with themes similar to Gundam, with Roberts setting Kong: Skull Island in the thick of the Vietnam War and Vaughn penning thematically deep comics like Saga and Y: The Last Man. Roberts and Vaughn eventually departed the project, but Mickle is no stranger to stories with big themes himself. Anyone who's watched Sweet Tooth can tell you that.

If Netflix tackles big themes in Gundam, it could launch a franchise that's action-packed and thought-provoking, and take Transformers' place as the giant robot movies to beat. A success would also give Sydney Sweeney a major win, cinematically; apart from the surprise success of The Housemaid and Anyone But You, she hasn't had much luck headlining major hits. But if Transformers has proved anything, it's that people love giant robots.

Being a fan of The Elder Scrolls is a lesson in patience as, at the time of writing, it has been fifteen years since the launch of the most recent entry, The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim and now, despite the next installment, The Elder Scrolls VI, being announced back in 2018, we are still waiting for that elusive release date, or even a release window.

However, despite Bethesda reportedly working hard behind the scenes, The Elder Scrolls VI is seemingly no closer to launch despite it being a priority for the studio after the launch of Starfield. Not only that, but with major studios such as BioWare shutting up shop in recent weeks, leading to Mass Effect 5 being canceled, fans are understandably worried that the same could happen for TES VI.

At the time of writing, The Elder Scrolls VI is still in development, but in the meantime, there is another exciting release to look forward to, and it arrives this month.

Courtesy of Zatu Games, The Elder Scrolls: Shadows of Oblivion is an upcoming board game inspired by The Elder Scrolls universe. Marketed for 1-4 players with each game lasting around 120-150 minutes, Shadows of Oblivion launches alongside unique componentry which allows players to adjust their gameplay experience, meaning that the replayability options are endless.

Retailing at just £20.99, The Elder Scrolls: Shadows of Oblivion's official item description reads as follows:

The Daedric princes rule their respective planes of Oblivion, and their influence over mortals cannot be understated.

Whether summoned to Tamriel for worship or study, these entities of great power will frequently strike deals and make pacts with those who dare.

Such a bargain is laced with poison and sure to bring misery, but a serious adventurer doesn't dismiss any potential advantage, and the prospect of wielding Daedric power is intoxicating!

Each of the five Daedric princes comes with something akin to a side quest, offering a blessing and a curse. It's recommended that adventurers play with both, but those looking to further manipulate the game's difficulty could choose one or the other.

What many may not know, however, is that The Elder Scrolls: Shadows of Oblivion actually serves as an expansion for Elder Scrolls: Betrayal of the Second Era's Heroes of Tamriel, the board game by Chip Theory Games that first launched back in 2025 following a successful Gamefound campaign. #3581. Sebastián Lelio, Chilean Director of Oscar-Winning ‘A Fantastic Woman,’ Dead at 52

Sebastián Lelio, the humanistic Chilean filmmaker whose trans drama “A Fantastic Woman” won the Best International Feature Film Oscar in 2018, has died at age 52.

The Chilean publication Emol first revealed the news that he was found dead in his home in Santiago on Friday, November 6, amid an undisclosed health issue. His body was discovered by his partner, the actress/director Amalia Kassai, who starred in his final film, the protest musical “The Wave” from Cannes 2025. Kassai also posted a statement in Spanish on her Instagram account.

Lelio was reportedly mid-production on the feature “Chilean Poet,” adapted from Alejandro Zambra’s Viking-published 2022 novel. Along with “A Fantastic Woman,” he also directed the Hasidic lesbian romance “Disobedience” in the same year, 2017; it starred Rachel McAdams and Rachel Weisz, and helped bring the filmmaker to international prominence. In 2013, he directed Paulina García to a Berlinale Silver Bear Best Actress win with “Gloria,” a late-in-life romantic comedy about a 58-year-old divorcee starting over again. He remade his own film in 2018 in English as “Gloria Bell,” released by A24 and starring Julianne Moore in the role García originated, opposite John Turturro.

Lelio regularly collaborated with the Chilean brothers Pablo Larraín and Juan de Dios Larraín, who served as producers on nearly all of his films. They were also collaborating with Lelio on his ongoing, now-final feature. Born in Argentina, he emigrated to Chile at age two with his mother and later graduated from Chilean Film School, after which he launched his career with short films and music videos. His debut narrative feature, “The Sacred Family,” premiered at the San Sebastián International Film Festival in Spain before his follow-up, “Navidad,” premiered at Cannes in 2009. The post-Chilean-earthquake drama “The Year of the Tiger,” starring beloved Chilean actor Luis Dubó, debuted at Locarno in 2011.

His fourth feature, “Gloria,” shot digitally and with a script and dialogue developed in part with his actors, including García, received U.S. distribution from Roadside Attractions and was widely regarded as one of the best films of 2013.

Lelio directed the first Best International Feature Oscar entry to win the Academy Award with 2017’s Golden Bear-nominated “A Fantastic Woman,” an exuberantly styled drama that put trans actress Daniela Vega on the international map. As Vega consulted on the script, it’s widely seen as a groundbreaker of trans portrayals onscreen in the 21st century. And it helped reform the perception and attitudes toward transness in Lelio and Vega’s home of Chile — and inevitably, within the Academy.

Lelio’s favorite films on the 2022 Sight & Sound poll included “La Dolce Vita,” “Playtime,” “The 400 Blows,” and “Singin’ in the Rain,” and you can feel their impact across his often irreverent, at times burstingly colorful, playful body of work.

His 2017 TIFF premiere “Disobedience” received U.S. distribution from Bleecker Street, and told the story of a forbidden, transgressive romance between two Orthodox Jewish women (McAdams and Weisz) in North London. The tender, taboo drama performed well in North America, grossing nearly $3.5 million domestic during a spring-through-summer 2018 run.

Lelio, that year, deftly remade “Gloria” as “Gloria Bell” with Julianne Moore as the free-spirited divorcee being wooed by John Turturro, and weighing choices in her next chapter living as a yoga instructor in Los Angeles. Returning to filming after the pandemic, Lelio broadened his collaborative scope to adapt “Room” author Emma Donoghue’s “The Wonder,” with Donoghue and Alice Birch co-writing the script with him. Florence Pugh starred as a British nurse sent to Ireland to observe a miraculous “fasting girl,” in a film that played Telluride and streamed on Netflix to strong reviews.

His last film, “The Wave,” took a minute to get off the ground after playing out of competition in Cannes 2025. The story of an introverted music student whose passion for protest is awakened amid a growing feminist movement on campus, “The Wave” received a small release from Wolfe Video earlier this year and received positive response throughout its festival run.

The status of Lelio’s final film isn’t known right now, but we can imagine that Lelio’s sensitive approach to character — and unstable identities finding their footing, their purest expression — will carry into the new work. The Larraín brothers were also producing the film, with Lelio’s regular cinematographer Benjamín Echazarreta on board as DP.

#3579. Could ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’ Re-Ignite Quentin Tarantino’s Bruce Lee Controversy?

It does not take long for the new trailer for “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” to invoke the most discourse-inducing scene from “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood.” In fact, the very first words we hear are “You heard the story about Bruce Lee getting his ass kicked by a stuntman?” Another reference to the Bruce Lee scene follows soon after, long before we hear any mention of Rick Dalton or any of the more consequential events of the first film..

The Netflix pseudo-sequel, directed by David Fincher and written by Quentin Tarantino, sees Brad Pitt reprising his Oscar-winning role as Cliff Booth. It’s billed as a separate adventure that happens to feature one of the film’s main characters — Leonardo DiCaprio is either completely absent or an incredibly well-kept secret, and Tarantino has said the film shares more DNA with Elmore Leonard’s paperback crime novels than the hangout movie style that defined the first film. But the marketing had to remind audiences who Cliff Booth is, and it’s curious that the second trailer’s primary reference point is a scene that is more memorable for the controversies it sparked than its role in the film’s plot. No mention is made, for instance, of the part Cliff played in dispatching several members of the Manson Family. Related Stories Sebastián Lelio, Chilean Director of Oscar-Winning ‘A Fantastic Woman,’ Dead at 52 Emily Feingold Hired as EVP, Communications for The Walt Disney Company

A brief recap for those lucky enough to have been offline during the original saga. “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” features a scene in which Cliff is left to hang around a TV set while DiCaprio’s Rick Dalton shoots an episode. While killing time, he ends up in a fight with Bruce Lee (played by Mike Moh). Neither man is particularly polite to the other, with Cliff appearing more interested in Lee’s sidekick role on “The Green Hornet” than his higher profile movie roles, and Lee quickly challenges him to a fight. Each man wins one round of the fight before it’s broken up, ensuring there’s no clear winner — but the mere fact that Cliff was able to throw a martial arts legend into the side of a car is a feather in his cap.

Following the film’s release, Bruce Lee’s daughter Shannon publicly objected to the way the film portrayed her father.

“It’s unfortunate because it has started this narrative in some places where some people are saying, ‘Oh, Bruce Lee was an asshole,’” Shannon Lee said in 2020. “Look, everybody can be an asshole sometimes. I can be arrogant and angry in my life — is that something I would say I am like generally? No, my father was not generally like that. He was extremely passionate and driven.”

She continued, “He could have a temper sometimes, but he did not go around challenging people to fights. Certainly not after he was a teenager. Anyway, he didn’t behave or boast in that way…My father worked extremely hard and directly toward the idea of authentic representation in Hollywood for an Asian man, so I don’t think he would’ve gone around beating up stunt people and that kind of stuff as a way of furthering his cause.”

Tarantino frequently defended the scene, saying that he based his fictional portrayal on real anecdotes about Lee from people who knew the actor.

“Bruce Lee was kind of an arrogant guy,” Tarantino said in a 2019 press conference. “The way he was talking, I didn’t just make a lot of that up. I heard him say things like that to that effect. If people are saying, ‘Well he never said he could beat up Mohammad Ali,’ well yeah he did. Alright? Not only did he say that but his wife, Linda Lee, said that in her first biography I ever read. She absolutely said that.”

The controversy still rears its head sporadically. During a 2021 appearance on “The Joe Rogan Experience,” Tarantino told critics of the scene to “suck a dick,” with the caveat that he understood why a daughter would object to any negative portrayal of her father.

By the time “The Futher Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” hits select theaters this month (and expands to Netflix in December), more than seven years will have passed since “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” premiered. Perhaps all parties have said everything there is to say about the Bruce Lee scene. But given how much the trailer leans into the matter, we could be in for another round of arguments about the portrayal.

#3578. Mass Effect’s Cruelest Moral Choice Remains Gaming's Most Haunting Mission 19 Years Later

Rebecca is a scientist-turned-storyteller and professional ghostwriter who enjoys forgetting common English words and making up her own in their stead. She's probably stuck between two basically-the-same dialogue options in a Larian game as you read this (there's so much at stake, obviously!!!). Rebecca currently lives with two gigantic puppies, a toddler consistently LARPing as Lara Croft, and her Halo-playing husband in Detroit, MI. You can find her past work at Zelda Universe and Verily Magazine.

Akuze looked like a gift: a lush world on the edge of Alliance space that had gone silent, a settlement standing intact with not one person left alive in it. Shepard’s patrol walked in and found nothing to fight. At first. But then, at nightfall, the ground opened. Thresher maws rose out of the earth, all teeth and tentacles, and when it was over, 50 marines were dead. Shepard was the only one who made it back to the landing zone. She took one rule from that night, because she needed it to be true: The dead have to count for something, or 50 people died for nothing.

So when, years later, an Alliance clerk told Shepard that a fallen marine named Nirali Bhatia “may save more lives in death than she did in life,” Shepard was faced with the decision — the opportunity — to make Nirali’s death count for something. Before the question ended, she was already agreeing. Hand a grieving husband his wife’s body? Or keep her for research that might save more lives down the line? Someone was going to pay for whichever answer I chose. (I knew Shepard would say yes. I also knew, thumbs hovering over the controller, that every part of me wished she wouldn’t.)

Back on the Citadel, after Tali joined the crew, Samesh Bhatia found us at the Presidium and apologized for the intrusion before he asked for anything. Samesh is a civilian, the husband of a marine, with no rank, no pull, and, by his own telling, nowhere else to turn. His wife, Nirali, was a marine in the 212. She died on Eden Prime, the colony where Shepard’s first mission in Mass Effect went hunting for a Prothean beacon and found the geth instead, attacking on orders of Saren Arterius, a rogue spectre operative. We found Ashley Williams there, at the dig site where her team had been posted, the last of her squad standing. Nirali didn’t make it off the planet, and the Alliance had refused to release her body. Samesh wanted to cremate her and give her a proper funeral. Ashley, who was in my squad on this run through Legendary Edition, had served in Nirali’s unit, which put two survivors of dead units on the Presidium, listening to a man who lost the one who didn’t make it.

Bosker — the clerk holding the case — waited in an embassy lounge. Nirali’s wounds didn’t match any weapon the Alliance had seen, he said, and so few bodies were intact enough to study that every sample counted. Shepard heard what survivors hear: If one body could buy a better defense against the geth, then maybe that person’s death doesn’t have to be wasted. A Sole Survivor needs to believe this more than anything.

I made the case to Samesh, and he said yes. He asked the Alliance to run its tests so that others would be spared the loss he feels, and he thanked us for finding him answers. A grieving husband thanked me for keeping his wife’s body. I took that as proof I’d done right.

Then nothing happened. The quest log closed, Samesh and Bosker disappeared from the Citadel, and that was Nirali Bhatia's farewell: a marine who died protecting a colony, filed under “completed.” A soldier had given everything on Eden Prime and would give a little more, so the Alliance could understand the geth sooner and maybe keep the next marine off the same table. That was the trade I told myself was fair. Samesh gave up his goodbye for it.

I thought I had done right, until I played out the other ending. This time, I leaned on Bosker instead, and he gave me a line I’d missed the first time: “Commander, you of all people should understand how far we go to protect humanity.” Shepard can answer, here, that none of that matters if we lose our humanity along the way.

And in that second playthrough, Shep (and I) realized something: Part of that, part of protecting our humanity, is protecting our right to ritual and our ability to say goodbye. Holding back the one body that might have kept other marines alive may have been the practical call, but Shepard had already watched 50 marines turn into easily forgotten numbers. This time, it was very clear that the most important thing to do was honor Nirali’s sacrifice by giving her rest, not a final mission. Bosker folded and released the body. I went back to deliver the news, still unsure if I’d made a better decision this time.

That uncertainty evaporated the second Samesh spoke. He said that saying goodbye would not bring him happiness, but it could bring him peace. Ashley told him that Nirali had loved him, that she’d missed his cooking, that she’d played recordings of him every night before bed. Hearing this, something in Shepard’s rule loosened.

In Mass Effect 2, if you let Samesh bury Nirali, you get an email. In it, Samesh thanks Shepard and tells her he'd opened the restaurant Nirali had planned, with free meals for Alliance personnel. In my first save, that restaurant never opened. In this one, it did. Maybe the dead have to count for something, and maybe sometimes that something is a husband who gets to be at peace — and a marine whose legacy counted most by going home.

#3577. Mickey’s Surprising Incompetence Balances Sheriff Country’s Excellence In Season 2

Cher Thompson is a Senior Staff Writer at Screen Rant, where she covers everything from explosive reality TV moments to cast interviews about the twists and turns of scripted dramas. With a background in creative writing, marketing, and teaching, Cher knows how to spot both the storytelling genius and the guilty pleasures in pop culture. Her work blends wit with insight, making readers feel like they’re chatting with a friend who just happens to know way too much about TV.

Despite Sheriff Mickey Fox (Morena Baccarin) often being good at her job, Sheriff Country season 2's crossover event made it clear that, even through a fantastic season, she can still have some level of incompetence. Throughout the run of the CBS spinoff, which just aired its first crossover event of the season with Fire Country, viewers have gotten the chance to see Mickey find her footing as Edgewater's sheriff. While Mickey dealt with difficulties in her personal and professional life, she's been able to prove herself throughout the show's run with good reads on both cases and those close to her.

While there's no doubt that Mickey is great at her job, it's been interesting to see her move through the issues in Edgewater throughout the early episodes of Sheriff Country season 2, especially as the show has thrown more in her way when it comes to her personal life. After mixing business and family throughout the first stretch of the season when Mickey's formerly presumed dead mother, DEA agent Eva Santos (Rachel Ticotin), was brought into the mix for a tough case, Mickey's judgment has been clouded more than once.

While her father, Wes Fox (W. Earl Brown), has always been making her life difficult, Mickey's had a difficult go of things this season, which has made it all the more interesting to watch her navigate her professional responsibilities. During Sheriff Country season 2 episode 5, "No Way In," Mickey's ability to remain professional was put to the test, and wavered more than it has in the past.

Although Mickey has long had to balance the difficulties of being a parent to her daughter, Skye (Amanda Arcuri), and handling the demanding side of her duties around Edgewater, the most recent episode of Sheriff Country saw her struggling to separate the professional and the personal. While Mickey did the noble thing jumping in to take Skye's place when she was being held hostage by a criminal who was out for the sheriff after a prison break, knowing she did it out of a personal risk as Skye's mother rather than a professional standpoint made it a tough decision to support.

Throughout the episode of Sheriff Country, it was clear that Mickey struggled to separate the nerves she was feeling about Skye being trapped at The Meat Up with a dangerous group of criminals from the ways she was handling the issue. While it was risky regardless of whether Skye was there or not, the fact that Mickey had to contend with her feelings as a mother made her feel more human in some regards, and threw her off her game entirely in others. It was clear that having Skye at risk was more difficult for the sheriff than anything she's faced before.

While Sheriff Country does a great job at showing Mickey balancing everything in her life well, the series needs to move on from the trope that's defined her character since the beginning of the series. Mickey is a complicated woman who deals with far more than most, but the fact that we as viewers rarely see her struggling with her decisions, emotions, or the realities of her life isn't a net positive. It's great that she can handle herself, but watching Mickey compartmentalize and vent her feelings, often to her sister Sharon Leone (Diane Farr) over a glass of wine, is growing tired.

Sheriff Country has allowed Mickey to be complicated enough of a character to support the fact that she may not always have everything together, and she definitely doesn't always know the right answers. Unfortunately, the show often makes it seem like Mickey is readily able to handle everything thrown at her, even if it's exhausting. Seeing her crack in some ways, even as she volunteered to allow a known criminal interested in killing her to take her hostage, was a refreshing shift for the series. Sheriff Country would be better to let Mickey continue to struggle, as it will make her rebounding all the more interesting.
