#3560. One of the Best QLED TVs of 2026 Is Over $1,300 Off Right Now

TCL has been pushing the boundaries of QLED TVs, making some of the best in the market at very competitive prices. This year, the company released its QM8L model, introducing a new design and impressive features and specs to a series that isn't even their flagship. Right now, the 65-inch QM8L is $1,197.99 (originally $2,499.99), $100 cheaper than it was just earlier this month, reaching its lowest price since it launched in April, according to price-tracking tools. Larger sizes are also seeing substantial discounts.

One of the first things you'll notice about the QM8L is the “Zero Border” bezel design, which gives it a modern, minimalistic look. When you turn it on, you'll likely note how bright this TV gets, which is a huge advantage QLEDs have over OLEDs. TCL claims it reaches 6,000 nits—seeing as the brightest OLED TV on the market only reaches 700 nits, no OLED can come close to this unit's brightness. Another important spec to note here is the local dimming zones: TCL claims this TV has up to 4,000, which means it gets top-tier backlight control, limited light blooming (thanks in part to TCL's "Halo Control"), and incredible contrast levels that some might not be able to distinguish from an OLED.

As many of us won't manually calibrate our TVs, the picture modes you can switch to in the settings will be most people's go-to. This TV's "Filmmaker mode" provides accurate color and picture, and if you're a gamer, you can use the native 144Hz high-refresh rate. If you don't already have a surround sound system at home and want to keep a minimalist setup, the QM8L comes with Dolby Atmos-ready Bang & Olufsen speakers, which offer above-average audio output compared to most TVs. You can read more about these features in CNET's 8.8/10 review. If 65 inches isn't quite right for your home theater setup, take a look at the QM8L's other sizes, which are also discounted right now.

#3559. PlayStation Plus Makes 10/10 Turn-Based Sci-Fi RPG Completely Free

If you have a PlayStation Plus Premium subscription, you may care to know that one of the very best RPGs of the PS2 generation is currently free with the subscription service. Better yet, it still completely holds up in 2026. Don't believe me? Go play it for yourself and out.

When it comes to PS2 RPGs, the bar is pretty damn high. Dragon Quest VIII: Journey of the Cursed King is still a complete masterpiece. Then there are some of the best Final Fantasy games ever made on the console. Of course, Square Enix aren't the only studio that makes RPGs, and there's one turn-based PS2 game that has never really had the love it deserves.

The PlayStation Plus library of PS1 and PS2 games isn't what it should be given how much a PlayStation Plus Premium subscription costs, but there are still some great games to be found there. One such game is the wonderful Rogue Galaxy. Developed by Level-5 (Ni no Kuni, Professor Layton), this 2005 sci-fi RPG remains, to my mind, a genuine 10/10 masterpiece. It's also managed to age beautifully, which is a rare feat for games of that era.

A big part of how the game managed to age so well should come as little surprise: the wonderful, timeless cel-shaded art style. Much like The Legend of Zelda: The Wind Waker, Rogue Galaxy's decision to go for a cartoon aesthetic over something more realistic has ensured it still looks incredible today. Its huge galaxy, which is made up of multiple planets, also remains a delight to explore.

Rogue Galaxy also delivers an epic tale with a wonderful cast of characters, which tends to be key for any good RPG. It wears its Star Wars influences on its sleeve, too. The game begins with a young farmer who becomes entangled in a galactic conflict, and ultimately becomes responsible for the fate of the cosmos. Definitely seen that somewhere before.

If you're looking for a sci-fi RPG that offers more fantasy elements, Rogue Galaxy is one of the best choices out there. It's much, much less serious and gritty than something like Mass Effect, but still able to deliver an emotional punch when it has to.

The only real thing to remember is that this is a two-decade-old game, and even while it's largely aged well, there are some rough edges. If you can roll with those punches, though, you'll get a brilliant 40-hour adventure in return. Not bad at all, right?

#3558. Eric Bauza’s Final ‘Looney Tunes’ Performance Is ‘Daffy Season,’ Now in Theaters Ahead of ‘The Cat in the Hat’

The death of Eric Bauza in October shocked the entertainment industry. An impressively prolific voice actor, it would’ve been nearly impossible for anybody engaging with animation over the past 15 years to never come across his work. Bauza’s death came just two months after the delayed release of “Coyote vs. Acme,” the “Looney Tunes” feature once deemed unreleasable by Warner Bros. Discovery and later sold off to Ketchup Entertainment. The film, which grossed $101 million worldwide, is a true showcase for Bauza, who lends his voice to a plethora of iconic characters, including Bugs Bunny, Daffy Duck, Elmer Fudd, Foghorn Leghorn, Tweety, and Porky Pig. Related Stories Box Office: ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Roars with $6.7 Million in Previews, ‘Ramayana: Rise of a Legend’ Earns $3.5 Million David Ellison’s Big Bet: Why the Mogul Thinks Skydance Film Chiefs Dana Goldberg and Josh Greenstein Can Deliver 30 Movies a Year

Bauza became something of the defining voice of modern “Looney Tunes” in his final years. Fans can see him give one final performance with the property in “Daffy Season,” a 7-minute animated short that plays before screenings of “The Cat in the Hat,” opening Friday from Skydance’s Warner Bros. Pictures. A representative for the studio confirmed to IndieWire that the short is Bauza’s final “Looney Tunes” movie. Bauza is also credited as providing additional voices for “The Cat in the Hat.”

“Daffy Season” centers on Daffy Duck, voiced by Bauza. He’s joined by Jeff Bergman as Bugs Bunny, Gabriel Iglesias as Speedy Gonzales, and Jeannie Tirado as Lola Bunny. The plot follows Daffy, turning his beak up at his fellow Tunes as they mindlessly obsess over the game of soccer. Todd Wilderman and Hamish Grieve are co-directors. “Daffy Season” is the first theatrically released “Looney Tunes” short since “Daffy’s Rhapsody” played before “Journey 2: The Mysterious Island” back in 2012.

Before “Daffy Season,” Bauza had already provided some voice work for a “Tunes” musical feature titled “Bye Bye Bunny,” which was canceled after some years of development and production. Other “Looney Tunes” credits from Bauza include the HBO Max series “Looney Tunes Cartoons” and the features “The Day the Earth Blew Up: A Looney Tunes Movie” and “Space Jam: A New Legacy.”

Bauza died at his home in Los Angeles on October 25 as a result of hypertensive cardiovascular disease. In a tribute in The Hollywood Reporter, Warner Bros. Pictures Animation producer Susan Rogers credited Bauza with playing a huge role in reviving the “Looney Tunes.”

“There wasn’t a single short he couldn’t quote or couldn’t reference,” she said. “I don’t think you replace Eric Bauza … The hole he leaves is huge. There are many talented people out there, and the franchise will move on. But there’s only one Eric Bauza.”

#3557. These Sony ANC Headphones Are on Sale for $128 Right Now

It's hard to convince yourself to spend nearly half a grand on premium headphones, like the Sony WH-1000XM6, even if you consider yourself an audiophile. Not everyone can afford those prices, which is why the budget, mid-tier, and premium tiers exist. While the premium 1000XM6 headphones are over three times the price of the mid-tier Sony WH-CH730N, they're not three times as good. The Sony WH-CH730N are $128 (originally $179) right now, the lowest price they've ever been according to price-tracking tools, and they offer an amazing value for your money.

It's pretty impressive what $128 in headphones gets you in 2026. The CH730N uses the same Sony Connect app as the premium headphones; as a result, you get a 10-band slider on the EQ menu, a battery care feature that extends the longevity of your battery life, 50 hours of juice, ANC, Ambient Sound (transparency mode), Multipoint to connect to two devices at once, and Bluetooth 6.0. The Adaptive Sound Control feature can detect your activity (walking, sitting down, loud environment, etc.) and automatically switch the level of ANC and transparency to make your experience as comfortable and seamless as possible.

The microphones are decent and use a feature to isolate your voice in noisy environments. I love that there's an AUX connection to give you the option, which seems to be coming back with newer headphones. The design is light and will feel like plastic, but they are comfortable to wear for long sessions. If you're looking to maximize the quality of headphones you can get for your money, the Sony WH-CH730N offer a pretty compelling option at $128.

Is there a better time than the weekend to kick back and relax with a nice film? We work all week, and having the chance to kick our feet up and watch a movie is the ultimate way to relax.

This week, I'm locked in on slightly older movies from the Prime Video new releases. We have a late 1980s cartoon that's extremely near and dear to my heart, a Christmas classic and a 2010s goofball movie that'll have you rolling on the floor laughing (assuming you have a tolerance for this sort of oddball humor).

These are the three new-to-Prime Video movies I think you should watch this weekend. There are only so many hours in a weekend, and you don't want to waste a bunch watching a bad film, so we'll guide you to the good ones.

I love "All Dogs Go to Heaven." It's a sad movie — both from a real-world perspective, given the circumstances of young actress Judith Eva Barsi, and from the plot involving the dog Charlie B. Barkin, his best friend Itchy Itchiford, and what happens to dogs when they die. But it's also heartwarming and highly entertaining for people of all ages.

Why is it special to me? As a kid, I went on vacation to Florida, and the day I arrived, I came down with a stomach bug that knocked me out of commission for the entire one-week trip. I literally did nothing but sit around in my grandparents' house for my entire annual vacation. And between trips to the bathroom, I watched "All Dogs Go to Heaven" over and over. You'd think that would make me dislike the movie, since I associate it with a ruined trip, but it brings back happy memories and got me through a difficult week. But it's not nostalgia; I watched it again as an adult with my 9-year-old stepson, and we both loved it.

Watch "All Dogs Go to Heaven" on Prime Video now

This is another throwback to my childhood — I guess I'm in a nostalgic mood today. But instead of associating this with sleeping on the bathroom floor, I remember watching it every winter to get ready for Christmas with the tale of Turbo Man (and sometimes in the middle of summer when I felt like throwing in a funny VHS).

Like many kids' movies, it all wraps up with a tidy bow in a completely unrealistic way, but that doesn't make it any less entertaining.

Watch "Jingle All The Way" on Prime Video now

I couldn't put only kid-friendly movies on the list, so the entirely not-child-appropriate "Hot Tub Time Machine" rounds it out. John Cusack, Rob Corddry, Craig Robinson, and Clark Duke contrast each other to create pure hilarity in this raunchy R-rated comedy, where the four go into a hot tub that sends them on a trip through time. It's a goofy premise for a goofy movie.

Keeping today's throwback theme alive, though, is the crew's first destination: 1986, the year I was born. If you remember the 80s fondly and want to see what a group of goofballs from 2010 do in the middle of the decade, you'll love this movie. It even has sci-fi elements that'll scratch fans' itch while keeping them laughing the whole way through.

#3555. New 4-Part Crime Thriller Officially Arrives on Netflix

The best crime dramas can keep audiences guessing about who committed a murder. But the truly elite? They're better off when they tell us what happens when it seems like the investigation is over. While shows like Mindhunter and True Detective have built enormous followings by exploring the darker corners of criminal investigations, one of the most critically acclaimed dramas of the 2010s took a much quieter approach. And despite earning the sort of reviews most television creators could only dream of, it somehow managed to remain relatively overlooked. Until now, perhaps.

All four seasons of Rectify have officially arrived on Netflix in the United States, joining the streaming service on November 1. The acclaimed drama originally aired on SundanceTV between 2013 and 2016, producing 30 episodes and earning widespread critical acclaim throughout its run, even winning one of the most prestigious awards going.

When Daniel Holden is released after nearly 20 years of complete isolation on Death Row, he returns as an outsider to his family, to his community, and to the times. Somehow, he survived the mental and emotional strain of his imprisonment, but now the walls have suddenly come crumbling down, and Daniel is set free in a world he no longer understands. He’s an outsider, lost in a once familiar world, struggling to navigate his newfound freedom. Combined with two decades of technological and social changes to his small town and the larger world, everything he encounters is a puzzle.

The cast stars Aden Young (The King Tide) as Daniel Holden, Abigail Spencer (Timeless) as Amantha Holden, Adelaide Clemens (Silent Hill: Revelation) as Tawney Talbot, Clayne Crawford (Lethal Weapon) as Ted Talbot Jr., J. Smith-Cameron (Succession) as Janet Talbot, Bruce McKinnon (Lawless) as Ted Talbot Sr., Luke Kirby (The Marvelous Mrs. Maisel) as Jon Stern, and Sean Bridgers (Get Shorty) as Trey Willis. The show is created by Ray McKinnon (Deadwood).

Rectify was met with universal acclaim from critics and audiences, receiving a score of 96% on Rotten Tomatoes, with the audience score not far behind at 92%. Its third and fourth seasons both earned perfect 100% critics' scores, while the final season achieved an extraordinary 99 out of 100 on Metacritic; it also received a coveted Peabody Award, which shows just how highly regarded it was.

All 30 episodes of Rectify, spanning four seasons, are streaming now on Netflix in the United States.

#3554. Focker In Law First Reactions Are Officially In

Focker-In-Law is already the talk of the town.

The Meet the Parents franchise is a multi-film comedy movie series centered on the cultural and lifestyle clashes between the uptight Byrnes family and the free-spirited Focker family. The franchise began in 2000 with the release of Meet the Parents, starring Robert De Niro and Ben Stiller, based on an independent movie released in 1992. Since then, two sequels have followed: 2004's Meet the Fockers and 2010's Little Fockers. After 16 years, Stiller and De Niro are returning to the beloved comedy.

Movie lovers and critics alike can watch the newest installment of the Meet the Parents franchise, Focker-In-Law, before its release on November 25. The new movie follows Greg Focker's (played by Stiller) son Henry (played by Skyler Gisondo) as he brings his trained FBI hostage negotiator girlfriend, Olivia (played by Ariana Grande), home to meet the family, leading to chaos and mayhem. First reactions to the iconic comedy franchise's return are officially in.

ScreenRant's Tatiana Hullender shared her thoughts on Focker-In-Law, praising Grande for meeting Stiller's stellar comedic timing in the best way by stating, "Focker-In-Law was such a fun and fresh movie! Seeing Ariana Grande go toe-to-toe with Ben Stiller was a blast, as Skyler Gisondo is adorkably lovable. Certified good time at the cinema!"

The Genre of Your Life podcast host, Doug Jones, shared a similar sentiment regarding Focker-In-Law, and even went as far to say that Grande "steals the show." "#FockerInLaw is a Focking good time! Perfect for the whole family & just in time for the holidays! Charmingly cute, hilarious & has a ton of heart. It captures everything that made the original so beloved & special. The new cast members are stellar & Ariana Grande steals the show," shared Jones.

The Grande praise keeps on coming, as writer and critic Bill Bria stated, "For the Ariana fans in my mentions: yes, she’s excellent in it. Proves that she gets the tone of the material. And, while she can be broad when it’s required, she’s mostly subtle and grounded, which sells the comedy even better." Bria continued and shared, "FOCKER-IN-LAW is the most unexpectedly pleasant surprise. Rather than lazily flipping the script of MEET THE PARENTS (or repeating it), John Hamburg & co. make a clever direct sequel that’s reliant on the top notch cast, with Ben Stiller being MVP. Some belly laughs in this one!"

Critic Christopher Rates It went so far as to state that Grande's presence would've been missed thanks to her charm and comedic timing. He stated:

"In all honesty, Focker-in-Law is funnier and better than you’d initially expect.

The combined chemistry of Ben Stiller, Robert De Niro, Ariana Grande, and Skyler Gisondo makes this just a simple fine watch to wind down. It feels reminiscent of the original and has some hilarious set pieces here and there but is ultimately bogged down by falling into legacy sequel tropes and some moments that feel out of place.

It’s a film that truthfully wouldn’t be the same without Ariana Grande’s charm, comedic timing, and ability to shift tones without it feeling jarring."

Editor and film critic Edward Douglas guarantees that laughter will arise when enjoying watching Focker-In-Law upon its global theatrical release on November 25. Douglas shared a post on X with a small review of the comedy movie and stated, "I just got back from an early screening of Focker-in-Law, and I was not expecting to laugh as much as I did, mainly because I'd seen the trailer so many times and was nervous those were the biggest laughs... nope... and the movie gives a lot more context to those jokes as well."

Another early review came from Brandon Davis gave for Focker-In-Law, which really makes clear that this is a perfect family movie by stating, "#FockerInLaw is a really fun time. It’s a bit over-the-top like a classic comedy at times and still reels it in for surprisingly touching end. Ariana is really good, Ben Stiller & Robert De Niro are committed & comedic as ever. My Mom is gonna love it."

That Hollywood Show's Editor-in-Chief, Junior Felix, goes as far as to claim Focker-In-Law is "the funniest films of the year." Felix shared his early thoughts on X and stated, "#FockerInLaw is one of the funniest films of the year! I had an absolute blast watching this film and genuinely was not ready for the amount of times I would die laughing. Ariana Grande is a damn treasure and has some hilarious moments. This is the pitch perfect family comedy we really need right now and it's the gift that keeps giving. Also, Eduardo Franco is HYSTERICAL!"

Amazon currently has the 32-inch Samsung Odyssey OLED G8 (G80SH) for $999.99, down from $1,299.99, and price trackers show that this is its lowest price so far. This is the newer 4K OLED model, not Samsung’s similarly named G80HS, which is a 6K IPS variant, and it makes the most sense for someone who wants one screen for both high-end gaming and everyday desktop use without moving to a larger ultrawide.

Its 4K QD-OLED panel runs at 240Hz, which gives the G80SH enough speed for competitive shooters and racing games while still keeping slower, more cinematic games looking sharp. You will need a powerful PC to get anywhere close to 4K at 240Hz, but the monitor is at least equipped for newer graphics hardware with DisplayPort 2.1 and HDMI 2.1. It also has USB-C with up to 98W of power delivery, so if this monitor doubles as a work setup, a compatible laptop can send video and charge over the same cable instead of adding another wire to your desk. FreeSync Premium Pro and G-SYNC compatibility should also help keep tearing under control, though OLED monitors can still show visible VRR flicker in darker scenes when frame pacing is inconsistent.

The bigger visual difference, though, shows up in darker games and HDR content, where blacks stay properly black and bright effects stand out without the blooming you often see on LCD monitors. That said, QD-OLED does have its own drawbacks, since blacks can take on a purplish tint in a brightly lit room, while burn-in remains a long-term concern—though Samsung does include active cooling and several screen-protection features to reduce uneven wear and says burn-in from normal use is covered under warranty. If you mostly play at lower frame rates or do not care much about OLED contrast, this is probably more monitor than you need, but for someone with the graphics hardware to take advantage of 4K at 240Hz, this discount makes the G80SH much easier to justify.

#3551. 10 of the Most Iconic Patrick Stewart Roles Beyond Captain Picard

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

Sir Patrick Stewart, an actor equally at home onstage at the Royal Shakespeare Company and on the bridge of the Starship Enterprise, has died at the age of 86. Unexpectedly for most of us, in part because he kept his final illness private, but more so because it once seemed as though nothing could fell the man who looms so large in our cultural consciousness.

The thoughtful, erudite performer who had a troubled childhood in working-class Yorkshire; the committed socialist who was eventually knighted by Queen Elizabeth; the advocate who put his money and his considerable voice toward the fights for LGBTQ+ acceptance and animal welfare and against domestic violence, his presence and performances meant the world (the galaxy, even) to myself and so many others. But those who knew him personally can offer better tributes; perhaps it's best left to Shakespeare's Player King, performed by Stewart himself opposite David Warner's Hamlet back in 1965:

Where joy most revels, grief doth most lament;Grief joys, joy grieves, on slender accident.

Much of Stewart's finest work was on the stage; other performances remain rather shockingly hard to come by (whither I, Claudius?). Nonetheless, he left a true legacy behind him, well beyond Captain Picard and Professor X. Here are 10 of his most iconic other roles.

A goofy, feel-good gay rom-com with the HIV/AIDS crisis still very much in the foreground, Jeffrey was a near-impossibility in the mid-1990s: a movie that neither villainized its queers nor treated them as pitiable martyrs. Steven Weber and Michael T. Weiss are the leads, joined by a cast that includes Christine Baranski, Victor Garber, Nathan Lane, Olympia Dukakis, and Sigourney Weaver but, for all those names, Stewart is the undeniable standout as Sterling, the irrepressible gay best friend: a swishing, mincing, sassy, high-camp character who steals every scene without ever becoming a caricature. He's the leader of the "Pink Panthers," a squad of queers who defend locals from gay bashers, and that is the key to the character's power: He's as gay as they come, but not ashamed and not even a little weak. This movie, and the presence of Captain Picard himself in it, might have saved my life back in 1995. Stream Jeffrey on Prime Video, Tubi, and The Roku Channel.

A sprawling, epic, and appropriately lusty take on the King Arthur stories from John Boorman, Excalibur is a mixed bag full of stunning visuals and iconic moments that never quite coalesce into something entirely coherent. Standing out among the film's many characters, Stewart is entirely memorable as Leodegrance, the boisterous, boorish, but ultimately faithful father of Guenevere who is among the first to pledge his loyalty to Arthur. Rent Excalibur from Prime Video.

Darcy Banker is erudite and intellectual, in his way, and even capable of charm, but otherwise has no redeeming qualities whatsoever. It's bad enough for the punk band Ain’t Rights that they've booked a last-minute gig at an Oregon bar without realizing that it's a haven for white supremacists. It's even worse when they witness a murder and become trapped in the title's green room, with Stewart as the lead skinhead. He's quite simply one of the all-time great (meaning absolutely terrifying) villains in this thriller that's pretty much a horror movie. Stream Green Room on Netflix.

Patrick Stewart's role as Professor Xavier in the X-Men is almost as pop-culture iconic as that of Captain Picard, spanning 26 years and nine movies, including the forthcoming Avengers: Doomsday. In most of those, he looks like he's having an awful lot of fun, but he gives his finest performance in the role in this elegaic installment, playing a dying Professor in profound cognitive decline, his dream in tatters and his bravado worn down to prickly dependence. We rarely get to see our superheroes at the ends of their days, and there's a lovely bravery to this depiction of the Charles' journey. Logan will likely be the toughest of his films to rewatch in the coming days. Stream Logan on Disney+.

This stagey television movie isn't the most sumptuous of the many filmed versions of the Dickens story, but you won't be surprised to learn that there are few better portrayals of Ebenezer Scrooge. It's rather a shame that Patrick Stewart didn't do more Dickens adaptations, since his booming voice and ability to play thoroughly heightened characters without ever resorting to caricature is as valuable as in Shakespeare. Rent A Christmas Carol from Prime Video.

Famously referred to as that "unknown British Shakespearean actor" when starting out on Star Trek: The Next Generation, Stewart was an associate of the Royal Shakespeare Company for twenty years before his most famous role came along. As is the way of live theater, much of his career lives on as an essential link in the chain of Shakespeare performances in the twentieth century...but not in a way that we can conveniently stream. We do, however, have this impressively mounted modern-dress stage production, in which Stewart plays King Claudius with characteristic brilliance against David Tennant's melancholy prince. Buy Hamlet from Prime Video and Apple TV.

As a cinematic actor, Stewart's greatest strength was bringing humanity to larger-than-life, even operatic roles, whether they be Arthurian knights, Dickensian villains, or superheroes. That ability is an absolute necessity if one is going to have any success doing Shakespeare, as Stewart did for decades. Match is something rather different, though, and it's rather lovely to see him play something just a bit more mundane—even if the film's Tobi Powell is a choreographer with a nearly legendary reputation. Teaching at Juilliard School, with his career winding down, he's confronted with the living embodiment of the past he left behind to pursue his career. The ensuing relationships grow more complex, with the film building to a climax that's surprising and deeply devastating, made all the more so by Stewart's muted, subtle performance. Stream Match on AMC+.

This is not the greatest Mel Brooks movie, not by a long shot, but it is a great comedic performance from Patrick Stewart. He loved to recount, with self-effacing embarrassment, the story of having shouted "We are not here to have fun" at his co-workers during a rowdy day on set at Star Trek: The Next Generation. By 1993, he was clearly past any such pomposity, and clearly having fun in his cameo as King Richard, a memorably silly take on a character he might well have played with seriousness elsewhere. Rent Robin Hood: Men in Tights from Prime Video.

Stewart's first real foray into science fiction was in this big, bold, divisive, and thoroughly bonkers Frank Herbert adaptation from director David Lynch. Stewart plays troubadour and warrior Gurney Halleck, and does what he does best: bringing gravitas and believability (and it must be said, bald sexiness) to even the wildest material. Stream Dune on Tubi.

Stewart plays an aged Merlin in this rather shockingly good modern reimagining of the King Arthur legendarium. His Merlin is all wild hair and rock band T-shirts, possessed of an essential kindness that makes him a valued mentor, and one deserving of his character's poignant farewell at the film's conclusion.Stream The Kid Who Would Be King on Disney+ and Prime Video.

#3550. Forget 'Fallout,' Netflix’s New Sci-Fi Western Officially Rides Onto Streaming

The Wild West has been the hope of some of the most notorious outlaws out there over the years but sometimes, outlaws or ordinary old gunslingers aren't quite enough for the story some people want to tell. And that's exactly the case with Netflix's latest series that mixes the sci-fi wasteland elements of Fallout and the adult adnimation of Arcane.

Netflix's new animated Sci-Fi Western Bass X Machina officially premieres on November 3, 2026, bringing an unusual blend of steampunk technology, supernatural horror, and Western action to the streaming service. Created by LeSean Thomas (Yasuke), the six-episode series features animation from Studio Mir, the acclaimed studio behind The Legend of Korra and The Witcher: Nightmare of the Wolf.

In a lawless Steampunk West overrun by brutal outlaws, machines, and supernatural terrors, a father is forced to become judge, jury, and executioner — knowing that every act of justice meant to protect his family may ultimately cost him the very people he’s fighting to save.

The voice cast is led by Brian Tyree Henry (Atlanta) as Bass, alongside Janelle Monáe (Glass Onion: A Knives Out Mystery) as Glory, Tati Gabrielle (The Last of Us) as Dana, Cree Summer (Rugrats) as Ahni, Chaske Spencer (The Twilight Saga: New Moon) as Lighthorse, Currie Graham (Reacher) as Rivenbark, and Starletta DuPois (The Notebook) as Etta.

The series is executive produced by Henry, Thomas, Jennifer Wiley-Moxley, and Chad Handley, with original music composed by Roman GianArthur Irvin and Nate Wonder through Wondaland. Netflix originally planned to release the show in October before shifting its debut to November.

Bass X Machina has also launched with a stunning 100% score on Rotten Tomatoes, which is a signal that the series is one to be taken seriously. In fact, by comparison, it is officially one of the best-reviewed Western television series of all time, as well as one of the highest-rated science fiction shows ever produced, not just by Netflix, but by any streaming platform. That puts it alongside some of the streamer’s most acclaimed animated originals, including Arcane.

#3549. Apple CEO John Ternus criticized for ‘scripted’ approach to first earnings call

Investors didn’t seem overly happy about yesterday’s Apple earnings call despite the record results. That likely reflects the company’s cautious take on margins in the current quarter, but some have also criticized what they describe as a very “scripted” approach by new CEO John Ternus.

Bloomberg was the biggest critic, describing it as a “timid” performance that left analysts “sorely disappointed” …

Apple investors and fans hoping to get an insight into the philosophy of new Chief Executive Officer John Ternus on Monday were left sorely disappointed. The 51-year-old’s first earnings call was a timid affair, with Ternus taking cover behind a carefully written script as analysts peppered him with questions.

Newly minted CEO plays it safe during his first high-stakes earnings call? Absolutely shocking! Seriously, what did Bloomberg expect?

Lee acknowledged that the slump in pre-market trading will have been largely driven by Apple’s caution about rising expenses in the current quarter. The company said that memory costs were continuing to rise and that building out Siri AI data centers we’re going to add to the RAM bill. But he argued that Ternus missed an opportunity to talk up the company.

In front of Ternus on Monday night was a chance to counteract the gloom and doom by instilling in Wall Street the fundamentals of the Ternus Doctrine — what he sees Apple becoming under his tenure, the “product guy” taking the company to a new era of innovation. Instead, he spoke like a man glancing at the clock and wishing the minutes away.

Fortune’s Sebastian Herrera was less vocal but echoed some of the criticism.

Ternus fielded some questions but also delegated answers to Chief Financial Officer Kevan Parekh and Chief Operating Officer Sabih Khan, who Apple said would participate in earnings calls moving forward, something the company hasn’t done for years. Ternus projected confidence on the call, but he appeared to stick mostly to scripted marketing points.

It will of course take Ternus some time to develop his own style when it comes to all of the varied aspects of the role, including addressing analysts in earnings calls, but I thought he took a measured but optimistic approach. Given the famously reticent style of his predecessor, the criticism strikes me as rather odd.

#3548. NBC Sets Up The End Of Network TV’s Longest Era

Cher Thompson is a Senior Staff Writer at Screen Rant, where she covers everything from explosive reality TV moments to cast interviews about the twists and turns of scripted dramas. With a background in creative writing, marketing, and teaching, Cher knows how to spot both the storytelling genius and the guilty pleasures in pop culture. Her work blends wit with insight, making readers feel like they’re chatting with a friend who just happens to know way too much about TV.

With its milestone 600th episode coming soon, Law & Order: Special Victims Unit is setting itself up for milestone after milestone, as well as the end of network TV's longest era yet. Having been on the air since 1999, Law & Order: SVU has become a cornerstone of NBC's slate of procedurals, stretching across decades and bringing even the most intense cases to life. From stories that are ripped from the headlines to intense character-driven cases, the series has become one of the most well-known and in-depth procedurals throughout its time on the air, building its own characters into the narrative.

With Mariska Hargitay's Olivia Benson becoming a fixture on the series quickly, the current Captain wasn't alone in the fight against New York's most heinous crimes. Throughout the earliest seasons of Law & Order: Special Victims Unit, Benson was partnered with detective Elliot Stabler (Christopher Meloni), who spent years on the series working alongside her. While Stabler left SVU in 2011, Meloni has returned to the series several times over the past 15 years, even anchoring his own series in the past few seasons, the now defunct Law & Order: Organized Crime. As one of SVU's defining characters, Stabler's one of Benson's closest connections.

With Organized Crime having come to an end on the heels of Special Victims Unit reaching a major milestone, Stabler's return to the series felt like kismet. It's also possible that his next reunion with Benson, during Law & Order: Special Victims Unit's 600th episode, could mark the end of one of NBC's longest and most agonizing eras.

While Stabler has returned to Law & Order: SVU in the past, seeing him in the upcoming 600th episode will be different for viewers, especially with this being his first appearance in the franchise post-Organized Crime. Stabler will be joining Benson in an investigation during Law & Order: Special Victims Unit season 28 episode 6, "Obedience," which will see the pair being tasked with revisiting one of their first cases together. As new leads come to light, Benson and Stabler will have to confront the mistakes and subsequent consequences of the choices they made in the past, which may change their present, too.

The premise of Law & Order: SVU's 600th episode calls into question the expertise of Benson and Stabler, and at the same time tasks them with an interesting new lens to look at their relationship from. While the professional aspect of having to retrace their steps from over 25 years prior is fascinating, bringing Stabler back into the mix to revisit a case is hardly the only thing that viewers will be anticipating from the episode. After years of slow-burning potential from Benson and Stabler, the chance to look at their past from a new perspective could give the pair a significant push forward.

While the episode doesn't necessarily have to turn romantic for Benson and Stabler, revisiting their past in a meticulous way could make for an interesting avenue for the characters to explore how things have changed. With their relationship consistently shifting and bending, the connection between the pair could find a new path during SVU's milestone hour.

For over a decade of Law & Order: Special Victims Unit, Benson and Stabler's partnership was close and personal, but never romantically charged despite some viewers hoping it would turn. Though Benson was typically single, Law & Order: SVU quickly established that Stabler was married with a family, and the series chose not to shift that dynamic to incorporate Benson into the mix. While Stabler's relationship wasn't always stable, it was clear that his partnership with Benson was a close connection that SVU wasn't going to complicate by putting romantic feelings on the table. Later, however, the series began to push a different agenda.

When Stabler's wife, Kathy, died prior to the launch of Law & Order: Organized Crime, a completely different path forward opened up for the Benson and Stabler connection. Now, long harbored respect and slow simmering romance was bubbling up to the surface, and it became clear that though there were never moments where the pair were going to act on those feelings prior, Benson and Stabler's chemistry was vastly different. Their relationship continued to grow more complicated as Benson and Stabler went through their own moments of hardship, but found one another there as support despite their professional tether all but snapping.

With Law & Order: SVU consistently bringing Benson and Stabler close to the brink of something more, even seeing the pair nearly kiss in a recent season, the former partners have never actually crossed that line. The 600th episode could be the perfect time for the former partners to try something new, especially with the show opening up their past to a completely different interpretation.

Though anything is possible in the world of Law & Order: Special Victims Unit, it doesn't necessarily feel like the show will ever truly feature Benson and Stabler in a supportive, happy romance, at least not in the way viewers might expect. While there's a compelling reason to push through and see Benson and Stabler finally pursue a relationship, the idea of putting the characters together only to have the bulk of their romance be off-screen doesn't offer the level of pay off that viewers would want. The tension between the characters, however, is still something that can keep the hope of a romance alive and well.

While there may not be a happy ending on the horizon for Benson and Stabler any time soon, the idea that something may shift between the characters in the Law & Order: SVU 600th episode isn't impossible. With a near-kiss already having happened on screen, there's a clear desire between the characters, and that points to something further taking place in the future, whether that's a near future or a far one. Hargitay has always spoken highly of Meloni and their work together, and bringing Stabler back into the mix almost always promises some great moments for the pair.

With a happy ending far from guaranteed, Law & Order: Special Victims Unit has always been in the habit of surprising its viewers, which could mean the Benson and Stabler story may well find itself changing for the better. Though it's not necessarily likely, it's definitely possible that Law & Order: Special Victims Unit's milestone episode could end the will they/won't they era for Benson and Stabler.

#3547. 10 Hacks for the Contacts App Every Apple User Should Know

The Contacts app is the bedrock of all my communication on my iPhone, and to a large extent, also on my MacBook. On the surface, Contacts appears to be a basic app that stores names, numbers, and other things you want to remember about people or businesses. However, it has some great features hidden under the surface, such as the ability to quickly delete duplicate contacts, smart lists, and faster ways to bulk share or delete contacts. Here are the 10 best Contacts app hacks for iPhone, iPad, and Mac:

If you have the same number or email address saved under multiple contacts, you can easily clear these from your iPhone. iOS shows you a prompt at the top of the list of contacts that lets you remove duplicate contacts easily. The same feature is hidden in the Mac version of Contacts. To try it, open Contacts on the Mac, and select the Card menu at the top of the screen. Then, click Look for Duplicates. This will identify duplicate contacts for you, and you can quickly merge or delete them.

It's pretty easy to select multiple entries when you use the Contacts app on the Mac. You can hold the Shift or Ctrl buttons and use arrow keys or click multiple contacts to select them all. On your iPhone or iPad, this feature is available via a hidden gesture. You need to use two fingers and swipe upwards or downwards on the list of contacts. Once you get the gesture right, you'll be able to select multiple contacts quickly. After you select one batch of contacts, you can scroll up or down and use the same gesture to add more contacts to your selection. This is the fastest way to execute bulk actions in your iPhone's Contacts app.

On your iPhone, you can use Contacts to message people on WhatsApp, Signal, Telegram, or other apps. Just open a contact and hold the messaging button. This will reveal a list of apps where you can ping that person. WhatsApp doesn't have access to my contacts, which makes it a bit annoying to message people I know. Since I started using the Contacts app to start chats on WhatsApp, the process of pinging new people has become a lot faster.

Just as you can use Contacts to message people on third-party apps, you can also use it to call them on those apps. Go to any contact in the Contacts app on your iPhone, and hold the call button. This will let you call them on WhatsApp, Signal, or any other apps where their phone number is linked.

iOS makes it hard to delete contacts quickly. This prevents accidental deletions, but it can be annoying when you just want to remove people who you last spoke to in high school. To speed this up, open Contacts on your iPhone and hold any contact's name. In the popover menu, select Delete to remove the contact. To remove multiple contacts quickly, use the two-finger swipe gesture to select multiple contacts, and hold any of the selected contacts. In the popover menu, you can select Delete X Contacts, where X is the number of contacts you've selected.

To export your entire address book, you can use the Contacts app on your Mac. Once you have it open, go to File > Export > Export vCard. This will save all your contacts in a vcf file, and you can import that into Google Contacts or other apps or services. You also have the option to export contacts as a PDF file. Just select File > Export as PDF to get it done.

When you create a new contact on your Mac, the app shows multiple fields that you may never use. If you just need to save phone numbers and email addresses, you can delete all the other blank fields from the template. To do this, open Contacts on your Mac, and go to Card > Add Field > Edit Template to add or remove fields from the default contact template.

If you added a number recently, such as a salesperson at a car dealership, but forgot their name, the Contacts app doesn't make it easy to find the contact. Instead of scrolling through the entire list of contacts and trying to guess which one could be the person you spoke to, you can use the Contacts app on your Mac to locate them quickly. It lets you create smart lists to sort contacts by recently added. Open Contacts on your Mac, and go to File > New Smart List. Now select Card in the first drop-down menu, followed by has changed in for the second one. You can then add the number of days, such as 10 days, in the final field, and click OK. Click the newly created smart list in the left pane, and you'll see all contacts that were either created or updated in the last 10 days, which will include the hypothetical car salesperson.

Smart lists also allow you to quickly create groups of related contacts. For instance, I've saved all my former colleagues' details with the company name in the contact. To find them all quickly, I created a smart list that groups all contacts with that company's name.

#3546. New iPad mini hands-on: Refreshed design, OLED display, more

Apple’s smallest iPad has gotten its biggest update in years. The new iPad mini features a much thinner and lighter design, a larger OLED display, water resistance, and the powerful A20 Pro chip.

I’ve been testing the new iPad mini, and there’s a lot to like — but also a couple of frustrations. Here’s everything you need to know.

The new iPad mini lives up to the “mini” name even more than its predecessor. It’s significantly thinner, down from 6.3mm on the previous iPad mini to 5.4mm on the new model. In fact, that puts it very close to the ultra-thin iPad Pro and the unfolded iPhone Duo. Here’s how it compares:

The new iPad mini is also significantly lighter, dropping from 293 grams to 255 grams. That puts it in the realm of the iPhone Duo, for comparison’s sake:

The reduction in weight and thickness was immediately noticeable when I picked up the new iPad mini. It feels significantly nicer to hold, more premium, and less “dense” in my hands.

The new iPad mini features an 8.5-inch screen, a slight increase from the previous generation’s 8.3-inch display. The overall footprint is mostly the same (the new model is actually about 2.2mm narrower). The larger screen is possible because the new iPad mini’s bezels are 24 percent thinner than before.

In addition to allowing a bigger screen in the same form factor, the narrower bezels also modernize the iPad mini’s overall look and feel. The bezels are noticeably slimmer than the iPad Air and base model iPad, and slightly thinner than the iPad Pro.

With smaller bezels, a thinner chassis, and a lighter weight, the new iPad mini feels significantly more premium than before. It reminds me less of the base model iPad or iPad Air and more of the iPad Pro, just shrunken down.

The big news about the display, though, is the switch to OLED. This marks Apple’s first non-Pro iPad to offer an OLED screen. It’s not the fancy tandem OLED display of the iPad Pro, but it’s a huge improvement over the previous model’s LCD panel.

The new iPad mini offers SDR brightness up to 600 nits, up from the previous model’s 500 nits max. The iPad mini also supports HDR content, with up to 1200 nits peak brightness.

The new iPad mini’s screen is undeniably an improvement over its predecessor. All of the inherent benefits of OLED apply here, including better colors, improved contrast, higher brightness, and more.

Unfortunately, the new iPad mini’s screen has one limitation: it doesn’t support ProMotion, or a 120Hz refresh rate of any kind. Instead, it’s still locked to 60Hz. This is an incredibly frustrating decision that I can’t quite wrap my head around.

Apple touts the iPad mini’s OLED screen as offering significantly faster pixel response time than the previous generation’s LCD panel, leading to improvements like smoother scrolling and reduced motion blur.

I’ve noticed that things like swiping between Home Screen pages, scrolling social media, and system animations are noticeably smoother. They aren’t, however, as smooth as an Apple device with a ProMotion display, and they’re not a substitute for a higher refresh-rate display.

I’m sure Apple knows the iPad mini’s market, and it seems to have decided not to prioritize ProMotion based on that information. However, as someone who has longed for a so-called “iPad mini Pro” for years, I’m disappointed by the decision. The new iPad mini’s screen is so much better … I just wish Apple had gone that extra step and added ProMotion. We’ve reached a point where ProMotion should be table stakes, especially after Apple brought it to the base iPhone 17 last year.

For an extra $100, you can upgrade the new iPad mini to have a nano-texture display (on the 256GB and 512GB models).

I’m a huge fan of Apple’s nano-texture display and have it on my 14-inch MacBook Pro. On the iPad mini, I think it makes even more sense.

The iPad mini is ultra-portable, and you naturally carry it around and use it in different lighting environments. The nano-texture glass helps reduce reflections and glare in a wide variety of lighting conditions. I also really like the combination of the iPad mini’s book-like size and the nano-texture finish.

There is a slight tradeoff in color vibrancy compared to a glossy OLED screen, as on other Apple devices with nano-texture, but it’s a very minor difference in my experience. The screen still looks fantastic.

One of the more interesting changes with the new iPad mini is something Apple calls the “Acoustic Display.” Instead of traditional speakers with visible grilles, Apple has developed a new system that uses the display itself to produce sound.

Essentially, Apple has designed special woofers that vibrate the display to produce low and midrange frequencies. For higher frequencies, custom tweeters are hidden between the glass and aluminum enclosure. Apple says this new system delivers louder audio, “punchier” bass, and clearer highs, despite the iPad mini’s significantly thinner design.

In practice, I think the new iPad mini sounds great. I’d choose headphones or an external speaker for serious music or video consumption, but day-to-day the iPad mini’s built-in speakers are perfectly adequate. (I’d bet that this Acoustic Display technology shows up in future iPhones too, and the iPad mini is serving as a test bed of sorts.)

The Acoustic Display also plays an important role in another major upgrade: water and dust resistance. The new iPad mini is IP67 rated, which means it can be immersed in 1 meter of freshwater for up to 30 minutes. It’s the first iPad to have an official water-resistance rating.

Adding water resistance to the iPad mini is particularly notable given its size and portability. I naturally find myself wanting to take it everywhere, and water resistance makes that more feasible.

One use case where all these improvements really come together is reading. The thinner and lighter design, nano-texture glass, and water resistance make the new iPad mini the most compelling iPad yet to serve as an e-reader.

The new iPad mini is powered by Apple’s A20 Pro chip, which I already covered in detail in my iPhone 18 Pro review. The short version: the A20 Pro chip gives you plenty of power for anything you can throw at the iPad mini today.

One detail worth calling out is that Apple uses two different versions of the A20 Pro in the iPad mini. The 128GB and 256GB models feature a five-core CPU and 16-core Neural Engine, while the 512GB model gets a six-core CPU and Dual 16-core Neural Engine. All three configurations feature the same seven-core GPU.

I don’t think anyone should buy the 512GB version of the iPad mini just for those extra cores. You should pick your iPad mini configuration based on how much storage you need, not the version of the A20 Pro chip. You don’t need to worry about performance with the new iPad mini. And perhaps most importantly, the A20 Pro chip ensures the iPad mini has enough headroom for the future.

There’s been a lot of consternation about where the iPad mini fits in a world where the iPhone Duo also now exists. It’s a fair question. After all, when the iPhone Duo is unfolded, the two devices share a similar form factor … but that’s really where the similarities end.

The iPad mini offers the full-fledged, unapologetic iPadOS experience. It supports the full multitasking prowess of an iPad Pro, including windowing and the menu bar. The new iPad mini also supports extended display mode, so you can plug it into an external display and extend your iPad experience there.

The iPad mini also gets iPadOS app layouts, and most importantly, a desktop-class browsing experience in Safari. It’s a remarkably capable device in a remarkably compact form factor. It fits where other iPads can’t, yet it runs the same version of iPadOS as other iPads.

The new iPad mini does all of that, but better than before. The thinner, lighter design paired with smaller bezels gives the new iPad mini a meaningful visual refresh. The added water resistance means you can do even more with the compact and pocketable iPad mini design.

But all of this comes at a higher price of $699. This marks the second price increase for the iPad mini this year. It started the year at $499, rose to $599 as part of Apple’s broader price increases in June, and is now $699 as of this refresh.

The new iPad mini also still starts with 128GB of storage. Increasing the base storage to 256GB would’ve helped ease some of the pain of that price increase. It’s also getting increasingly hard to manage a device with 128GB, particularly with the storage needs of Apple Intelligence and Siri AI. The lack of ProMotion and Face ID also make the price increase sting more.

Ultimately, the iPad mini form factor is a joy to use. The design feels great in the hand, and having the full iPadOS experience in such a compact device remains impressive. It’s not quite the “iPad mini Pro” I’ve always wanted, but it’s big upgrade to a form factor that I’ve always loved.

Aside from the best foldable phones, I tend to see a lot of innovation around rugged phones built for long-term off-grid living or weekend camping getaways.

I’ve tested my fair share of unconventional ones: from the projector-packing Blackview Xplore 2 all the way to the Sonim XP Pro Thermal with its Predator-like heat vision. Every single one brought something wild to the table, but the Oukitel WP63 packs something I genuinely haven't seen before: a built-in electronic fire igniter.

While most phone manufacturers design their hardware specifically to avoid catching fire (ahem, Note 7), this heavy-duty slab embraces it for emergency survival. Honestly, it’s one of the most interesting rugged phones I’ve come across this year.

If the igniter alone isn’t enough to convince you, it also packs a massive 20,000mAh battery, a built-in reverse-charging cable, an all-in-one camping lantern, and a night vision camera.

Best of all, it’s currently 43% off for a limited time, dropping the price from $599 down to $339.

Built for extreme off-grid adventures, the Oukitel WP63 features an emergency electronic fire igniter, massive 20,000 mAh battery, built-in reverse-charging cable, 6.67-inch 120Hz display, rear camping lantern, and an 8MP night vision camera to see through the darkness.

The integrated lighter on the Oukitel WP63 brings back memories of the push-in cigarette lighters found in old-school cars. The heating element is tucked away on the top edge of the phone, popping open to reveal the recessed coil with a light press. Through the dedicated Lighter app, I can trigger the ignition process, which quickly causes the coil to glow with that familiar cherry-red warmth.

It generates concentrated heat capable of sparking dry materials on direct contact — like scrap paper or dried-up leaves that have been baking under the sun. For safety reasons, the igniter enforces an automatic cooldown period of around 10 seconds to prevent the housing from overheating.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

While I was genuinely surprised by how easily it lit the corner of an envelope, keep in mind that nursing that spark into a sustainable fire takes real effort. Because it doesn’t produce an open flame like a Bic lighter or butane torch, having prior campfire-building experience makes a huge difference. After several tries, I managed to get a small bundle of brittle autumn leaves to catch, but it definitely requires patience and bone-dry kindling.

Beyond its standard 64MP main shooter — which delivers respectable shots when lighting conditions cooperate — Oukitel also throws in a dedicated 8MP infrared night vision camera. For a rugged phone built for the backcountry, it’s an invaluable tool the moment true darkness sets in.

While dedicated night vision cameras I’ve tested offer superior performance, especially in how far their IR illuminators can reach, the WP63’s sensor is still ideal for scanning your immediate vicinity for critters rustling in the brush. If you're out camping, it's especially handy when you have to step out of your tent half-asleep in the dead of night and your eyes haven't yet adjusted to the blackness.

Even though the setup is limited to just a single main camera and a night vision lens, the quality from the primary sensor more than suffices for the quick run-and-gun shots I want to share on social media. And the selfie camera up front isn’t too shabby, either.

As much as I rely on the flashlight on my phones, they’re dinky compared to the blinding beam produced by the WP63’s rear-mounted camping light. At its brightest, it effortlessly illuminates an entire pitch-dark area, and it has serious endurance thanks to the massive 20,000 mAh battery packed inside. With hurricane season in full swing, I’m confident it could easily hold up through an extended power outage. On top of that, an emergency strobe function unleashes an intense beacon that can be spotted from long distances.

I also want to highlight the 3W loudspeaker mounted on the back, which completely puts flagship phone audio to shame. While most phones tend to distort heavily at maximum volume, this speaker delivers surprising low-end punch and clarity — making it feel like I’m carrying a dedicated Bluetooth speaker in my pocket.

The Oukitel WP63 is an unlocked phone ready to run on virtually any wireless carrier, and I love that it features one of the easiest SIM card slots to access without hunting down an ejector pin.

This Swiss Army knife approach works because it nails the practical essentials for off the grid excursions — headlined by its halo feature, the built-in igniter. That utility is backed by smart additions like an integrated USB-C cable, allowing it to double as a ready-to-go power bank for other gear.

Tipping the scales at over 1.3 pounds, it’s certainly not a device I’d want as my primary everyday carry. But as a secondary backup? It’s an easy sell, especially while it's 43% off. Whether you toss it into a glove compartment for road trips or pack it along for a weekend in the woods, the Oukitel WP63 delivers rugged peace of mind when facing worst-case scenarios.

#3544. Apple explains the $400 premium for the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display

Apple argued that the touchscreen isn’t the headline feature of the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display, merely a bonus.

The headline should instead be the quality of the display itself – with the company effectively suggesting that the $400 premium is positively cheap for what you’re getting …

Apple published a white paper in which it argues that the latest MacBook Pro display is essentially a smaller version of its professional reference monitor, the Studio Display XDR.

$400 for the screen and new design isn’t my issue, my issue is the cost of storage and memory. $600 more to go from 24gb to 48gb or nearly a grand for 64gb. You can easily spend nearly double the cost of the machine just getting it to a semi-future proof spec.

Given that this costs anywhere from $2,899 to $3,599 just for a display (albeit a significantly larger one with a correspondingly higher resolution), this does put into perspective that $400 extra over the MacBook Pro with the standard screen. Here’s what Apple has to say about it:

PROLED XDR display, the best display in a pro laptop, finally overcomes these historic limitations. For the first time, a MacBook Pro display uses tandem OLED technology, delivering up to 1000 nits of sustained full-screen brightness, 2000 nits of peak high dynamic range (HDR) and standard dynamic range (SDR) brightness, and a 10,000,000:1 contrast ratio with accurate, per-pixel black levels.

It’s driven in real time by an all-new display engine in M5 Pro and M5 Max, which continuously compensates each pixel for content, usage, temperature, and ambient conditions—delivering creative precision out of the box and protecting panel lifespan over time. And a unique manufacturing process ensures panel-to-panel consistency and minimizes off-axis color shift, a first for any OLED laptop.

As Macworld spotted, that’s almost identical to the company’s description of the the Studio Display XDR.

In fact, the PROLED XDR in the MacBook Pro is the only display other than the Studio Display XDR that supports Apple CMF 2026, the next generation of CIE 1931. Apple says CMF 2026 “more precisely aligns the appearance of the display with an ideal D65 illuminant—the standard reference for white—and significantly improves appearance matching across display technologies, which is important for workflows that use multiple displays side by side.”

Resolution aside, the other specs are identical with just one exception: the contrast ratio. As for that exception, the MacBook display comes out on top with a 10 million to 1 contrast ratio, in contrast with the Studio Display XDR’s one million.

Does this change your own perspective of the price premium of the OLED model? Please share your thoughts in the comments.

#3543. 10 Perfect Miniseries Based on Books, Ranked

It was in the UK back during the '50s and '60s that the miniseries format was born, still named "television serials" before the term "miniseries" was coined in the US in the '70s. Indeed, it was American networks who adopted, rebranded, and greatly popularized the format precisely around that time. Since then, the small screen has offered hundreds upon hundreds of masterful miniseries worthy of being counted among the greatest shows of all time.

Though many of those exceptional miniseries have been fully original stories, many others have been adapted from previously-existing material, including several books. It could be a miniseries based on a great, foundational classic of literature, such as 1995's Pride and Prejudice; or one based on a non-fiction book about much more modern events, like Dopesick. Regardless, these are some of the best miniseries of all time.

Before the American remake became the first-ever Netflix original series, the BBC adapted Michael Dobbs' House of Cards, the first political thriller novel in the trilogy of the same title. This is the story of Conservative Party chief whip Francis Urquhart, a Machiavellian politician who rises to power right after the end of Margaret Thatcher's tenure as Prime Minister of the UK.

It's also one of those rare screen adaptations whose quality surpasses that of the source material.

It's far and away one of the greatest British miniseries of the '90s, with a career-defining performance by Rian Richardson and some absolutely perfect use of fourth-wall-breaking. What's more, it's also one of those rare screen adaptations whose quality surpasses that of the source material. The show perfectly captures the Shakespearean qualities of Dobbs' book, while adding plenty of its own unique spice.

Elizabeth Gaskell's 1854 novel North and South is a true cornerstone of Victorian literature, and it has been adapted for the small screen thrice. There's a strong argument to be made in favor of the fourt-part version starring Richard Armitage and Daniela Denby-Ashe being the best of the bunch, as it perfectly recounts the story of a privileged young woman relocating herself to an industrial mill town, where her initial clash with a stern cotton mill owner slowly transforms into a deep romance.

The sizzling chemistry between Armitage and Denby-Ashe practically oozes through the screen in every scene they share; which, combined with the show's top-tier production values and nuanced writing, makes for an absolutely faultless adaptation of one of the most acclaimed English-language Victorian novels. Both those who love the source material and those who have never read it should love this incredible miniseries.

She was already a well-known name in Hollywood by the time Netflix's The Queen's Gambit came out, but it was this exceptional miniseries that really launched Anya Taylor-Joy into serious, award-worthy superstardom. This is based on Walter Tevis' 1983 novel, following an orphaned chess prodigy battling addiction and personal demons as she rises through the male-dominated ranks to become an international grandmaster.

It's one of the best Netflix shows with less than 40 episodes, bolstered by the incredible writing just as much as it is by Taylor-Joy's unforgettable turn as Beth Harmon. It's a mesmerizingly complex antihero story that makes every chess movement feel like an element from an adrenaline-pumping thriller, greatly elevating the entertainment value of the source material while staying quite faithful to its narrative skeleton.

Four Netflix characters, four completely different ways of showing up for somebody. This is the one who fits how you actually do friendship, and what having them in your life would be like.

You do not do friendship at half volume, and neither does he. What you want is somebody who says yes to the plan before you have finished describing the plan.

You are the friend who makes things happen, and so is she. Together you would be mildly exhausting to everyone around you and completely delighted with yourselves.

You have no patience for pleasant lies, and she has no ability to tell them. What looks like coldness from the outside is the most reliable friendship on this list.

You look after whoever is having the worst day. So does he. It is the least strategic way to move through the world and the best possible quality in a friend.

By this point, Mike Flanagan has already firmly established himself as one of the modern kings of horror television, but even the greats have to start somewhere. In his case, that was his first-ever show: The Haunting of Hill House, based on Shirley Jackson's 1859 novel, about a family forced to reunite years after their mother's mysterious death after another tragedy draws them back to the mansion that still holds them captive.

Many would go so far as to say that it's one of the best miniseries ever made, which makes it unsurprising that it turned Flanagan into such a household name. There are hugely effective elements of horror, but what really fuels the story is the emotional and thematic depth of its narrative. It may not be all that faithful to Jackson's classic in terms of plot, but it captures the book's spirit marvelously.

Kevin Sullivan's CBC classic Anne of Green Gables can be viewed as either a two-part miniseries or a made-for-television film. Regardless, one thing remains certain: This is a cornerstone of televisual Canadian pop culture. Based on the eponymous book by Canadian icon Lucy Maud Montgomery, the miniseries follows a spirited orphaned girl who's taken in by an aging brother and sister on Prince Edward Island, her fierce charm slowly transforming their lives and the local community.

Though its DNA is as passionately and warmly Canadian as that of Montgomery's book, this is as universally endearing of a small-screen story as they come, full of exceptional performances and breathtaking PEI and rural Ontario vistas. It's the sort of miniseries so irresistibly charming and emotionally complex that it's virtually impossible to watch it and not enjoy it at least a little bit.

The subject of both the Hulu masterpiece Dopesick and the non-fiction book it's based on, Dopesick: Dealers, Doctors, and the Drug Company that Addicted America is the story of the company that triggered the worst drug epidemic in American history. What follows that premise is one of the best crime miniseries of all time, one as insightful as it is deeply human and admirably dramatic.

How can one even begin singing the praises of such a perfect show? For one, there's the star-studded cast, featuring top-tier performances by actors like Michael Keaton and Kaitlyn Dever. Then, there's the multi-perspective framing, which lends the story an air of raw realism. All in all, it's an incredible adaptation that fuses the journalistic spirit of its source material with deeply sensitive and faithful narrative drama.

The question of what single book is most worthy of the elusive title of "The Great American Novel" is a debate that's probably destined to never have one satisfying answer, but there's a certain title that's thrown around far more often than most: Larry McMurtry's Lonesome Dove. This just so happens to be the source material of the greatest Western TV miniseries the world has ever seen.

One of the best 8-episodes-or-less masterpiece miniseries in history, Lonesome Dove is both deeply faithful to the legendary book and uniquely strong when analyzed in a vacuum. It's a masterful de-mythologization of the American Frontier and the tropes it carries with it, anchored by Basil Poledouris' incredible music and the jaw-droppingly perfect work of stars like Robert Duvall and Tommy Lee Jones.

Jane Austen's Pride and Prejudice, about the eventful relationship between the quick-witted Elizabeth and the wealthy Mr. Darcy, is such a crucial pillar of English literature that adapting it is always a titanic task. In the eyes of many fans, no one has ever been more successful than Andrew Davies, whose BBC adaptation is far and away the most perfect version of the story that the screen has ever been graced with.

One of the miniseries with the most perfect pacing and most wonderful writing, Pride and Prejudice mainly benefits from Colin Firth and Jennifer Ehle displaying some of the most unbelievable chemistry that any actor-actress duo has ever displayed in a miniseries. Full of iconic moments, luxurious visuals, and loving fidelity to Austen's classic, it's a must-see for anyone who doesn't have a heart of stone.

Based on the historical novels I, Claudius and Claudius the God by Robert Graves, the BBC's I, Claudius is one of those near-perfect miniseries that have been tragically forgotten as the years have passed. Nonetheless, this retelling of the history of the early Roman Empire from the perspective of Emperor Claudius still remains one of the highest-rated miniseries in history on IMDb.

That praise is all for good reason. It's an absolutely brilliant adaptation that marvelously condenses two super-complex novels into a seamless 12-episode narrative, darkly satirical and absolutely Shakespearean in tone. On top of being visually and narratively impressive, it's also a masterclass in classical acting, including the top-notch performances of actors like Derek Jacobi, John Hurt, and Patrick Stewart.

For years, HBO's Band of Brothers, executive-produced by Tom Hanks and Steven Spielberg, has been the highest-rated miniseries of all time on IMDb. It's such a masterful show that that's likely to never change. Based on the 1992 non-fiction book of the same title by historian Stephen E. Ambrose, it's one of the best-ever HBO miniseries based on books, and then some.

There's the incredible performances of the stacked cast, including actors of the stature of Damian Lewis, David Schwimmer, Michael Fassbender, and Tom Hardy. There's the way the show, much like Hanks and Spielberg's Saving Private Ryan, captures the brutality of World War II combat with unmatched realism and humanism. There's the deep emotional resonance of the way the book explores themes of brotherhood and leadership. From top to bottom and from beginning to end, Band of Brothers is not only an immensely faithful adaptation of an excellent non-fiction book, but genuinely one of the greatest works in television history.
